t: NoSQL data models: document, key-value, wide-column and graph, and how to model for each
sum: What each NoSQL model stores and why, and how modelling changes when the database cannot join: access-pattern-first design, embedding versus referencing in documents, partition and clustering keys and bucketing in Cassandra (Discord's message store), DynamoDB single-table design with GSIs, key-value structures in Redis, property graphs and traversals, and the consistency trade-offs that come with each.
prereq: db1
Entities, relationships and keys; one-to-many and many-to-many relationships; foreign keys are enforced inside one database.
db2
Normalization removes redundancy; denormalization copies data for read speed and needs a maintenance mechanism.
sc8
When to choose relational, key-value, document, wide-column, search, graph or time-series stores, at the system-design level.
sc7
Partitioning by key, hot partitions and why cross-partition queries are expensive.
why:
In early 2015, Discord built its first version in under two months and stored everything in a single MongoDB replica set. By the end of 2015 it held 100 million messages, and by early 2017, when the company published "How Discord Stores Billions of Messages", users were sending more than 120 million messages a day, and Discord had promised to keep every one forever. MongoDB's index on (channel_id, created_at) no longer fit in memory, latency had become unpredictable, and the team needed a database that could absorb an endless, accelerating stream of writes while still answering one query instantly: "show me the latest messages in this channel".

They chose Cassandra, a wide-column database, and the interesting part of their story is not the choice but the modelling. Cassandra has no joins, no ad-hoc secondary access paths worth relying on, and no way to scan a table efficiently by anything other than its key. So the key had to be designed around the query. Their first design used the channel as the partition key, which immediately produced warnings: some channels' partitions were over 100 MB, because a busy channel lives for years and its partition grows forever. The fix was to add a time bucket, about ten days of messages, to the partition key. Then came surprises no relational database would have produced: a message that was edited and deleted at the same moment came back as a half-empty row, because every Cassandra write is an upsert resolved by last-write-wins; and writing null into unused columns created twelve deletion markers per message, which slowed reads.

This is the core of NoSQL modelling. Relational design (db1, db2) starts from the entities and their relationships, normalizes them, and trusts the query planner (db7) to answer whatever questions come later. Document, key-value, wide-column and graph databases each give up some of that generality to make particular access patterns fast at scale, typically by storing together the data that is read together and by partitioning it across machines by key. The price is that you must know your queries first, that data is often duplicated across several shapes, and that consistency guarantees are usually weaker or need explicit choices.

The system-design lesson sc8 covered when to choose each kind of store. This lesson is about how to model data once you have chosen one: what each model physically stores, how to turn access patterns into documents, partition keys, sort keys, data structures or graph edges, and which mistakes each model punishes. It works through MongoDB embedding, Discord's Cassandra tables, DynamoDB single-table design, Redis structures and property graphs, with a running example of storing an LLM chat product's conversations in each.
primer:
From "store the facts" to "store the answers"

A relational database is like a well-organised library of facts. Each fact is filed once (normalization), and the librarian, the query planner, can assemble any answer you ask for by fetching and combining facts from different shelves. That flexibility is wonderful, but it has a cost at very large scale: combining facts from different shelves means joins, and when the shelves are spread across hundreds of machines, joins become network traffic and coordination.

NoSQL databases are more like a set of pre-packed answer boxes. If the most common question is "what's in this order?", you pack each order, with its lines and shipping address, into one box, and answering the question means fetching one box. If the most common question is "what are the latest messages in this channel?", you keep each channel's messages in one sorted pile on one machine, and answering means reading the top of the pile. Fetching one box or one pile is fast and scales: different boxes live on different machines, and no question needs more than one machine.

The analogy breaks, usefully, when the questions change. A library of facts can answer a new question with a new combination. A warehouse of pre-packed boxes can only answer the questions it was packed for; a new question ("which orders contain product 42?") may need a second set of boxes packed differently, which means writing the same facts twice and keeping both copies in step. That is the central trade of NoSQL modelling: reads are designed in advance, and writes pay for it.

The four models in one sentence each

A key-value store maps a key you can construct to a value or a small data structure. A document store stores self-contained nested documents, the natural shape of an aggregate such as an order or a conversation. A wide-column store stores partitions of rows sorted by a clustering key, spread across machines by a partition key, built for enormous write volumes keyed by entity and time. A graph database stores nodes and relationships as first-class records, built for queries that walk relationships. The rest of this lesson is how to model well in each.

What you give up, and what you get

It helps to be explicit about the trade before modelling. You usually give up joins at read time, ad-hoc queries on arbitrary fields, multi-record transactions by default, and the database's enforcement of relationships (there are no foreign keys between documents or partitions). You get predictable single-digit-millisecond reads for the patterns you designed, near-linear horizontal scaling by adding machines, very high write throughput (especially in LSM-based wide-column stores), flexible record shapes, and, in managed services, little operational work. Whether that trade is good depends entirely on whether your important access patterns are known, stable and key-shaped. When they are, NoSQL models are simple and fast; when they are not, every new question becomes a remodelling project.
body:
1. The method: access patterns first

Every NoSQL modelling exercise starts the same way, and it is the step people skip. Write down the access patterns: each read and write the application performs, with its inputs, outputs, ordering, expected frequency and latency target. For the chat product used throughout this lesson:

#Access patternInputFrequency
A1List a user's conversations, most recent first, 20 per pageuser idevery app open
A2Load the latest 50 messages of a conversation, in orderconversation idevery conversation open
A3Append a message to a conversationconversation id, messagevery high
A4Find the owner of a conversation (for authorization)conversation idevery request
A5Count messages per model per day (analytics)date rangedaily

Then, for each important pattern, design so that it is answered by a single read: one key lookup, one partition range read or one document fetch. Patterns that cannot be served that way get their own copy of the data (a second table, an index, a summary) or are moved elsewhere: analytics like A5 almost always belong in a warehouse fed by a change stream (db12), not in the operational NoSQL store. This is the opposite of relational design, where you model the domain and trust indexes and joins to answer queries later. It is not worse, just a different contract: in exchange for planning, every listed query has predictable latency at any scale.

2. Document stores: aggregates, embedding and referencing

A document store (MongoDB, Couchbase, Firestore; also PostgreSQL's jsonb when used this way) stores each record as a nested document, typically JSON or its binary form BSON, addressed by an id, with indexes on fields inside the document. The modelling unit is the aggregate: a cluster of data that is created, read and updated together, such as an order with its lines and shipping address. Storing the aggregate as one document means one read to load it and one atomic write to change it, since single-document writes are atomic.

The central decision is embedding versus referencing. Embed when the child data is owned by the parent, read with it, bounded in size and not shared: an order's lines, a user's addresses, a conversation's settings. Reference (store an id and fetch separately) when the child is shared by many parents (a product referenced from many orders; embedding would copy it everywhere and make updates painful), large, unbounded (a post's comments, a channel's messages), updated independently at a high rate, or queried on its own. Unbounded arrays are the classic document-model failure: MongoDB documents are limited to 16 MiB, each append rewrites the document, and reading the parent drags the whole array along.

For the chat product, embedding all messages in the conversation document is tempting and fails on exactly those grounds: a long agent session can contain thousands of messages, including large tool outputs. The robust design uses the subset pattern: a conversations collection with owner, title, timestamps and the last few messages embedded (enough to render a preview), and a messages collection with {conversation_id, seq, role, content, created_at} and an index on (conversation_id, seq). A1 becomes an indexed query on {owner: uid} sorted by updated_at; A2 an indexed range read on messages; A3 an insert into messages plus a small update of the conversation's preview and timestamp.

Two more document-modelling ideas recur. Schema versioning: documents in one collection can have different shapes, so include a schema_version field and migrate lazily on read or in background batches. Validation: MongoDB supports JSON Schema validators on collections, which restore some of the guarantees a relational schema gives for free; use them for required fields and types.

3. Key-value stores: structures, not just values

A key-value store maps keys to values, and every read starts from a key the application can construct. Pure key-value stores treat the value as an opaque blob; Redis, the most widely used, offers data structures as values, which changes modelling considerably. A hash holds a small record's fields (HSET conv:c2 title "sql help" owner ana), readable or updatable field by field. A list or stream holds an ordered sequence (recent messages, a job queue). A sorted set holds members ordered by a numeric score, which makes A1 natural: ZADD user:ana:convs 1759500000 c2 on every update, then ZREVRANGE user:ana:convs 0 19 returns the 20 most recent conversation ids. Sorted sets also implement leaderboards, sliding-window rate limiters and time-ordered feeds. Keys can carry a TTL (time to live), so sessions and caches expire automatically.

Key design is the whole schema: a consistent naming convention (type:id:subtype) is the closest thing to table definitions, and every access path is a key you can compute. That makes key-value stores ideal for session state, caches, counters, rate limits, feature-flag lookups and the online half of a feature store (hd8), and poor at anything needing queries by value. Redis is primarily an in-memory store, so data size is bounded by RAM and durability depends on its persistence configuration; it is usually paired with a durable system of record rather than replacing one.

4. Wide-column stores: partitions and clustering keys

Cassandra, ScyllaDB and Google Bigtable (and HBase) are wide-column stores. Discord's post gives the best short description: Cassandra is a "KKV" store. The first K, the partition key, is hashed to decide which nodes store the data (with replication, several nodes). Within a partition, rows are identified and sorted by the second K, the clustering key, and each row holds named column values (the V). A partition behaves like a sorted dictionary on one node, stored in LSM-tree SSTables (db5). The efficient operations are: read one row by full key; read a contiguous slice of a partition by clustering-key range; write anything (writes are append-only upserts and are very cheap).

Modelling is query-first, one table per query. For A2, the partition key must contain the conversation (or channel) id, because the query supplies it, and the clustering key must order messages by time. Discord's first design was exactly that, PRIMARY KEY (channel_id, message_id), with message_id a Snowflake id (a 64-bit id whose high bits are a timestamp, so ids sort by creation time and two messages created in the same millisecond still have distinct keys). The Cassandra schema, slightly simplified:

CREATE TABLE messages (
  channel_id bigint,
  bucket     int,
  message_id bigint,
  author_id  bigint,
  content    text,
  PRIMARY KEY ((channel_id, bucket), message_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message_id DESC);

The bucket came from the problem in the introduction. Cassandra can technically hold huge partitions, but Discord saw warnings for partitions over 100 MB and learned that large partitions put pressure on garbage collection during compaction and cluster expansion, and cannot be spread across nodes. A channel lives forever, so a partition keyed only by channel grows forever. The fix is bucketing: add a coarse time window to the partition key, derivable from the message id or timestamp. Discord looked at its largest channels and chose roughly 10 days per bucket to stay comfortably under 100 MB. The lab's arithmetic shows why the bucket width depends on traffic: at about 1 KB per stored message, a channel with 1,000 messages a day fills 100 MB in about 105 days, one with 50,000 a day in about 2 days. A read of "latest 50" computes the current bucket, reads from it, and if it returns fewer than 50 rows (a quiet channel), moves to the previous bucket, and so on. Discord accepted that quiet channels need several reads, because active channels, the majority of reads, find enough messages in the first bucket.

Patterns that need a different key get a different table. A1 (a user's conversations) needs partition key user_id and clustering by last activity, so it is a second table, written alongside the first. Cassandra offers materialized views and secondary indexes to do this automatically, but both have operational caveats (views have had consistency problems; secondary indexes query every node for each lookup), so most teams write both tables from the application, often in a logged batch.

5. Writes, deletes and consistency in Cassandra

Two behaviours from Discord's post are essential to modelling correctly. First, every write is an upsert and conflicts between replicas are resolved by last-write-wins per column, using write timestamps. Cassandra discourages reading before writing, so an UPDATE of one column on a row that a concurrent request deleted simply creates a row containing that column and the key. Discord saw exactly this when an edit raced a delete: a message row with text but no author, which crashed code expecting the required field. Their fix was to treat rows missing a required column as deleted and clean them up. Designs should assume any column may be absent and avoid patterns where correctness depends on reading a value and writing back a modified one; for the rare operations that truly need compare-and-set, Cassandra's lightweight transactions (based on Paxos) exist, at several times the latency of a normal write.

Second, deletes are writes. Because replicas may be temporarily unreachable, a delete must be remembered so it can be replicated, so Cassandra writes a tombstone, which reads skip and compaction removes only after gc_grace_seconds (10 days by default). Writing null to a column is a delete and creates a tombstone too. Discord's message schema had 16 columns, of which the average message set only 4, and their code wrote nulls for the other 12: twelve tombstones per message, for nothing. Writing only non-null values removed them. Delete-heavy patterns, such as using a Cassandra table as a work queue, accumulate tombstones that reads must scan, and Cassandra aborts queries that encounter too many, so queues belong in a queue system or in a database with in-place deletes.

Consistency is tunable per request: with replication factor 3, writing and reading at QUORUM (2 of 3 replicas) guarantees a read sees the latest acknowledged write (sc6 covers quorum arithmetic), while ONE is faster and may return stale data. Choosing per access pattern, QUORUM for messages a user just sent, ONE for analytics-grade reads, is part of the model.

6. DynamoDB: partition keys, sort keys and single-table design

Amazon DynamoDB is a managed key-value and document store whose primary key is either a partition key alone or a partition key plus a sort key. Items with the same partition key form an item collection, stored together and sorted by sort key, and a single Query can return a range of them (sort key equals, begins with, between, greater than). Items are limited to 400 KB. Throughput is spread across physical partitions, each of which, per AWS's documentation, delivers at most 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second, so a single partition key value can never exceed those rates, however much table capacity is bought.

Because DynamoDB has no joins, a popular technique called single-table design stores several entity types in one table under generic key attributes (PK, SK) chosen so that data read together shares a partition key. For the chat product: the user's profile is PK = USER#ana, SK = PROFILE; each of her conversations is PK = USER#ana, SK = CONV#2026-10-03#c2, with the date first so the sort key orders conversations by time; each message is PK = CONV#c2, SK = MSG#0001. A1 is one Query on PK = USER#ana in descending sort order, returning the profile and the conversations together. A2 is one Query on PK = CONV#c2 with SK begins_with MSG#. The lab emulates this with a SQLite table whose primary key is (pk, sk), and its query plans show each pattern as a single range search on the key.

A4 (who owns conversation c2?) needs a lookup by conversation id, which the main key does not support. A global secondary index (GSI) gives the table a second, independently partitioned key: putting GSI1PK = CONV#c2 on the conversation item lets a Query on the GSI find it, and the item's main key reveals the owner. GSIs are maintained asynchronously, so reads from them are eventually consistent, and they consume their own write capacity, since every item written that has the GSI attributes is also written to the index. A table may have up to 20 GSIs by default. The same machinery models many-to-many relationships with the adjacency list pattern in AWS's guidance: one item per edge, keyed by one side, with a GSI keyed by the other side, so both directions are a Query.

Single-table design is powerful and often over-applied. Its benefits are real when entities are read together at high scale. Its costs are a table no human can browse, entity logic encoded in string prefixes, and difficulty adding access patterns later, since a new pattern may need a new GSI and a backfill. Separate tables per entity are perfectly reasonable when entities are accessed independently.

7. Hot partitions and write sharding

All partitioned stores share one failure: a hot partition, where one key gets a disproportionate share of traffic. Examples: a viral post's like counter, a celebrity's follower list, a table keyed by today's date so all of today's writes hit one key, a single global "settings" item read on every request. In DynamoDB the per-partition limits make this concrete: a key written more than 1,000 times a second (for items up to 1 KB) will be throttled. Remedies follow a pattern. Choose high-cardinality partition keys that spread naturally (user id, not country). Write sharding: append a suffix to hot keys (LIKES#post9#0 … #9), write to a random shard, and read all ten and sum, trading read cost for write spread. Cache hot reads in front of the store. And avoid time-only partition keys for write-heavy data; combine time with an entity or a shard number. The chat product has a natural hot-partition risk in agent sessions that stream hundreds of small token updates per second into one conversation: buffer tokens and write the message once it completes, or write chunks every few hundred milliseconds rather than per token.

8. Graph databases: relationships as data

A property graph stores nodes (with labels such as User, Account, Device, and key-value properties) and relationships (typed, directed, with their own properties, such as (:User)-[:OWNS {since: 2024}]->(:Account)). The physical trick that makes graph databases different is index-free adjacency in engines like Neo4j: each node record points directly to its relationships, so following an edge costs a pointer dereference rather than an index lookup in a join table. A traversal's cost therefore grows with the number of edges actually visited, not with table sizes.

Queries are pattern matches. In Cypher, "accounts connected to a flagged account through shared devices or cards, up to four hops":

MATCH (bad:Account {flagged: true})-[:USED|PAID_WITH*1..4]-(other:Account)
WHERE other <> bad
RETURN DISTINCT other.id;

The same query in SQL is a recursive CTE (db4) over edge tables with cycle protection, joining whole tables per hop, which the planner struggles to estimate. Graph models suit fraud and risk networks, recommendations ("people who bought this also bought"), access-control inheritance through groups, network and dependency analysis, and knowledge graphs used alongside vector search in retrieval-augmented generation, where entities and their relations extracted from documents are stored as a graph and traversed to gather context. They suit poorly: bulk aggregations over all nodes (a warehouse does those better) and simple one- or two-hop lookups, which relational indexes handle just as well with simpler operations.

9. Choosing the model from the access patterns

With the four models understood, the choice for a given workload can be reasoned rather than guessed. Take each access pattern and ask what shape the answer has. If the answer is "one record by an id I already have" and nothing else, a key-value store is the simplest fit. If it is "one self-contained aggregate with nested parts, sometimes filtered by fields inside it", a document store fits. If it is "a time-ordered slice of a very long, write-heavy sequence keyed by an entity", a wide-column store fits. If it is "everything reachable within a few hops along typed relationships", a graph fits. If the patterns are varied, change often, need ad-hoc filtering and aggregation, or need transactions across entities, a relational database fits better than any of them.

Apply that to the chat product. A1 and A4 are key lookups with a small sorted list; A2 and A3 are a write-heavy, time-ordered sequence per conversation; A5 is analytics. At modest scale (millions of messages a day), a relational database answers all five with two tables and three indexes and is the right choice. At Discord's scale (well over 100 million messages a day, kept forever), A2 and A3 dominate and justify a wide-column store, while A1 and A4 can live in the same store as separate query tables or in a key-value store, and A5 moves to a warehouse fed by change data capture. The model follows the dominant access pattern at the scale you actually have, and different parts of one product legitimately use different models.

10. Keeping duplicated data consistent

NoSQL designs duplicate data deliberately: the same conversation title in the user's list and in the conversation item, the same message in a per-channel table and a per-user table, a comment count in the post document. Each duplicate needs a defined write path, the same discipline as relational denormalization (db2). The options, from strongest to weakest: a transaction across items where the store supports it (MongoDB multi-document transactions, DynamoDB TransactWriteItems for up to 100 items, Cassandra logged batches for atomicity without isolation); writing the source of truth first and updating copies from a change stream (DynamoDB Streams, MongoDB change streams, Cassandra CDC), which is eventually consistent but robust; or best-effort dual writes from the application, which drift under failures and need a reconciliation job. Choosing per duplicate, and writing the choice down, is part of the model.
deep:
Why these models partition well

The common thread of document, key-value and wide-column stores is that each record or partition is self-contained and addressed by a key, so the system can hash the key to a machine and never needs to coordinate across machines for a single-key operation. This is what the aggregate-oriented view (popularised by Sadalage and Fowler) captures: an aggregate is a natural unit of consistency, distribution and access. A relational join or a multi-row transaction crosses aggregates, which in a partitioned system means crossing machines, needing distributed coordination (two-phase commit or consensus, db8 and sc9). NoSQL systems either forbid such operations, make them explicit and expensive (DynamoDB transactions, MongoDB distributed transactions), or provide weaker guarantees. Distributed SQL databases (Spanner, CockroachDB) take the opposite path, keeping relational semantics and paying for coordination with consensus and careful data placement. Understanding this lets you predict which operations any store will make cheap: the ones that stay within one aggregate.

LSM storage underneath wide-column stores

Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase and Bigtable all store partitions in LSM trees (db5), which explains several modelling rules. Writes are cheap because they go to a memtable and a commit log, so write-heavy, append-mostly data fits naturally. Reads of a partition may need to merge several SSTables, so a partition whose rows were written over a long time and frequently updated costs more to read than one written once; time-bucketed partitions are written mostly within their window and then become immutable, which keeps reads cheap. Deletes are tombstones by necessity, since data is never updated in place. And time-window compaction strategies drop entire SSTables when all their data has expired, so data with a TTL and time-bucketed keys is cheap to expire, whereas row-by-row deletes are expensive. Good wide-column models align partitions with how data is written and expired.

The cost model of a DynamoDB design

DynamoDB bills reads and writes in units tied to item size: a strongly consistent read unit covers one read per second of an item up to 4 KB (an eventually consistent read costs half), and a write unit covers one write per second of an item up to 1 KB. Two consequences shape models. First, item size matters: a 20 KB item costs 5 read units per consistent read and 20 write units per write, so splitting rarely needed large attributes (a long prompt, a tool output) into a separate item or into S3 cuts cost for the common reads. Second, every GSI that includes an item is another write, so projecting only needed attributes into GSIs and avoiding unnecessary GSIs saves money directly. A Query that reads 50 small messages in one item collection is billed by total size read, rounded up to 4 KB, so item collections of small items are efficient. Reasoning in capacity units is the DynamoDB equivalent of reading a query plan.

Multi-model and convergence

The categories are blurring. PostgreSQL with jsonb, GIN indexes and pgvector is a competent document and vector store with SQL and transactions around it; MongoDB has multi-document ACID transactions, joins via $lookup, schema validation and vector search; DynamoDB has transactions and, recently, vector indexes; Redis has modules for JSON documents and search; graph query languages are being standardised as GQL (ISO, 2024), and SQL itself gained property-graph queries (SQL/PGQ) in SQL:2023. The practical consequence is that the choice is less about which model a product can express and more about its storage engine, scaling model, consistency guarantees, operational maturity and cost at your access patterns. Model the access patterns first; then the product choice is usually clear.

Schema evolution without a schema

Changing a NoSQL model is a data migration even though no DDL is run. Adding an optional field is easy: old documents simply lack it, and code handles both. Changing a key structure (a new partition key, a different sort-key format, a new GSI attribute) requires rewriting every affected item, usually by backfilling with a scan in batches while the application writes both old and new forms, then switching reads, then cleaning up: the same expand-contract pattern as relational migrations (db14), but without database support for online index builds in some stores and with capacity costs for the backfill. Versioned documents (a v attribute) and readers that tolerate multiple versions make these migrations survivable. This is the hidden cost behind "schemaless": the schema exists in every reader, and every reader must be updated.
prod:
Discord's migration, as a production pattern

Discord's 2017 migration is a template worth knowing in detail because each step generalises. They modelled from the one critical access pattern (read recent messages by channel), chose a key that served it with one partition read, and discovered the unbounded-partition problem during the import, not in production, because they loaded real data first. They dark-launched: the application wrote to both MongoDB and Cassandra and read from both, comparing, before any user depended on Cassandra; that surfaced the null author_id bug from last-write-wins before it reached users. They found the tombstone waste by looking at what was actually being written. And they accepted a known trade-off (quiet channels need more bucket reads) after measuring that most reads hit active channels. Discord later moved the same data model from Cassandra to ScyllaDB, keeping the key design; the modelling outlived the database.

Common production failures by model

Document stores: documents that grow without bound (embedded arrays of comments, events or messages) until writes slow and the 16 MiB limit is hit; missing indexes causing collection scans that look fine in development; and inconsistent document shapes after years of schema drift, crashing readers that assumed a field. Key-value: memory exhaustion and evictions in Redis when keys lack TTLs; a single huge key (a sorted set with millions of members) blocking the single-threaded server during large operations; and cache stampedes on hot keys. Wide-column: large partitions, tombstone-heavy reads, hot partitions, and slow repairs. DynamoDB: throttling on hot keys; scans used as queries (a Scan reads and bills the whole table); GSIs with insufficient capacity throttling writes to the base table; and costs dominated by oversized items. Graph: "supernodes" with millions of relationships (a celebrity, a default device id shared by many accounts) that make every traversal through them explode, needing degree limits or modelling changes.

Observability that matters

For each store, a few metrics map directly onto modelling problems. Partition-level metrics: DynamoDB's CloudWatch Contributor Insights shows the most accessed and most throttled keys; Cassandra's nodetool tablehistograms and table statistics show partition size distributions and tombstones scanned per read. Document stores: slow-query logs and plans showing collection scans; document size distributions. Redis: memory usage, evictions, keyspace hits and misses, and the slow log for large-key operations. Track these against the access-pattern list: each pattern should have a latency and cost budget, and a regression usually traces to one key, one partition or one document shape.

AI workloads on NoSQL

Several AI-system components map naturally onto these models. Online feature stores are key-value lookups by entity id with strict latency budgets (hd8), commonly on Redis or DynamoDB, fed by batch and streaming pipelines; the hot-partition and item-size rules apply directly. Chat and agent state is an append-heavy timeline per conversation, the Discord pattern, with the added twist of very large items (tool outputs, retrieved documents, images) that should be stored in object storage with pointers. Caches of LLM responses keyed by a hash of the prompt and parameters are classic key-value with TTLs. Knowledge graphs for retrieval store extracted entities and relations as a property graph, traversed to expand context around retrieved chunks. And vector search, increasingly offered inside these same stores, adds its own modelling questions (filtering, tenant isolation) covered in db15. In each case the method is the same: list the access patterns, design one cheap read per pattern, and define how duplicated data stays consistent.
myths: NoSQL means schemaless, so you don't need to design a schema.

The schema still exists; it has moved from the database into your code and your key design. In DynamoDB or Cassandra the keys you choose decide which queries are possible at all, and changing them later means rewriting the data. NoSQL modelling usually needs more up-front design than relational modelling, not less.
Document databases can't do relationships.

They can reference other documents by id and look them up, and MongoDB has $lookup for joins in aggregations. What they make cheap is data that is read together being stored together. Relationships that are many-to-many, frequently queried from both sides, or need integrity across documents are where the relational model is stronger.
In Cassandra you model the entities, then add indexes for the queries.

You model the queries. Each table is designed to answer one query pattern with one partition read, and the same data is often written to several tables with different keys. Secondary indexes exist but query every node for low-cardinality values, so they are a last resort.
Graph databases are just for social networks.

Any data whose valuable queries follow relationships of unknown or variable depth fits: fraud rings linking accounts by shared devices, supply chains, access-control inheritance, knowledge graphs for retrieval. If your queries are mostly one or two hops, a relational database with indexes on the join keys usually does as well.
Single-table design in DynamoDB is always the best practice.

It makes multi-entity reads of one item collection a single query and avoids joins, which matters at very high scale. It also makes the table hard to read, hard to evolve and awkward for analytics. AWS's own guidance has softened to 'use it where access patterns benefit'; several tables are fine when entities are accessed independently.
A key-value store is a hash map with persistence, so it can't model anything complex.

Redis offers sorted sets, hashes, lists, streams and more, so leaderboards, rate limiters, queues and time-ordered feeds are natural; and DynamoDB is a key-value store with sorted sort keys, which supports rich modelling. The limit is that every query must start from a key you can construct.
lab:
Goal: size Cassandra time buckets from traffic, and emulate DynamoDB single-table design with a composite-key B+ tree to see each access pattern become one range read. Python 3.12 standard library. Save as db11.py.

import json, sqlite3

# Part 1: bound Cassandra partition size with time buckets (Discord-style)
MSG_BYTES = 1_000                        # average stored size per message, overhead included
LIMIT = 100 * 2**20                      # keep partitions under ~100 MB
for per_day in (1_000, 50_000, 500_000):
    days = LIMIT / (per_day * MSG_BYTES)
    print(f"channel with {per_day:>7,} msgs/day: one partition fills 100 MB in {days:8.1f} days")

# Part 2: a DynamoDB-style single table emulated with a composite-key B+ tree
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE items (pk TEXT, sk TEXT, gsi1pk TEXT, gsi1sk TEXT, data TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (pk, sk)) WITHOUT ROWID")
db.execute("CREATE INDEX gsi1 ON items (gsi1pk, gsi1sk)")      # a 'global secondary index'
rows = [
    ("USER#ana", "PROFILE",               None,           None,          {"name": "Ana"}),
    ("USER#ana", "CONV#2026-10-01#c1",    "CONV#c1",      "META",        {"title": "trip plan"}),
    ("USER#ana", "CONV#2026-10-03#c2",    "CONV#c2",      "META",        {"title": "sql help"}),
    ("CONV#c2",  "MSG#0001",              None,           None,          {"role": "user", "text": "hi"}),
    ("CONV#c2",  "MSG#0002",              None,           None,          {"role": "assistant", "text": "hello"}),
    ("USER#raj", "PROFILE",               None,           None,          {"name": "Raj"}),
]
db.executemany("INSERT INTO items VALUES (?,?,?,?,?)", [(*r[:4], json.dumps(r[4])) for r in rows])

def query(sql, *args):
    plan = " | ".join(r[3] for r in db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + sql, args))
    out = [(pk, sk) for pk, sk, *_ in db.execute(sql, args)]
    print(f"   {out}\n   plan: {plan}")

print("A1 user profile + conversations, newest first (one partition, one range read):")
query("SELECT pk, sk, data FROM items WHERE pk = ? ORDER BY sk DESC", "USER#ana")
print("A2 messages of conversation c2 in order:")
query("SELECT pk, sk, data FROM items WHERE pk = ? AND sk BETWEEN 'MSG#' AND 'MSG#~'", "CONV#c2")
print("A3 which user owns conversation c2 (inverted lookup via the GSI):")
query("SELECT pk, sk, data FROM items WHERE gsi1pk = ?", "CONV#c2")

What to look for.

  1. Part 1: at about 1 KB per message, a 100 MB partition holds about 105 days of a 1,000-message-a-day channel but only about 2 days of a 50,000-a-day channel, and a few hours of a 500,000-a-day one. Bucket width must be set from the busiest channels, which is how Discord arrived at about 10 days.
  2. A1 returns the profile and both conversations, newest first, from one item collection; the plan is a single SEARCH … USING PRIMARY KEY (pk=?).
  3. A2 is a range on the sort key within one partition: (pk=? AND sk>? AND sk<?).
  4. A3 uses the emulated GSI to go from conversation id back to its owner, the inverted access path.

Try next. Add a fourth access pattern, "all conversations created on a given day across all users", and notice that no existing key serves it; design a GSI for it and think about whether a date-only key would create a hot partition (it would: add a shard suffix). Then change Part 1 to 4 KB messages with large tool outputs and see how bucket widths shrink, which is the argument for moving large payloads out of the row.
recap: NoSQL databases trade the relational model's flexible queries and joins for data layouts that make specific access patterns fast and that partition easily across machines.
Without joins, modelling starts from the list of access patterns: each important query should be answered by reading one key, one partition or one document.
A document store keeps aggregates as nested documents; embed data that is read together and bounded in size, and reference data that is shared, large, unbounded or updated independently.

A wide-column store such as Cassandra uses a partition key to choose the node and a clustering key to sort rows within a partition; tables are designed per query and partitions must stay bounded, for example by time buckets.

DynamoDB's partition key and sort key support single-table design, where related items share a partition key and range queries on the sort key fetch an item collection in one request; global secondary indexes provide other access paths.
Key-value stores like Redis model data with structures (hashes, sorted sets, lists, streams) and every read starts from a known key.
Graph databases store nodes and relationships as first-class records, so traversals of variable depth cost per edge followed rather than per join over whole tables.
Denormalization is the norm in NoSQL, so every duplicated fact needs a write path that keeps copies in step, and most stores offer weaker or tunable consistency.
Discord's 2017 move to Cassandra keyed messages by ((channel_id, bucket), message_id) with roughly 10-day buckets to keep partitions under 100 MB.
glossary: A specific way the application reads or writes data, such as 'latest 50 messages in a channel'; NoSQL schemas are designed from the list of these.
A cluster of related data treated as one unit for reads and writes, such as an order with its lines; the natural unit of a document.
Binary JSON: MongoDB's binary encoding of documents, with extra types such as dates and 64-bit integers.
Adding a coarse value such as a time window to a partition key so that no single partition grows without bound.
Reading a database's committed changes from its log and publishing them to other systems.
In Cassandra, the part of the primary key that orders rows within a partition and identifies a row inside it.
A declarative query language for property graphs that matches patterns of nodes and relationships.
A database that stores self-describing nested documents (JSON or BSON) addressed by id, such as MongoDB.
Storing related data inside the parent document instead of in a separate document or table.
A DynamoDB index with its own partition and sort key, maintained asynchronously, giving an alternative access path.
A partition receiving a disproportionate share of traffic, limited by the throughput of the single node or shard that holds it.
In DynamoDB, all items that share a partition key value, readable together with one Query.
A database that maps keys to opaque values or simple structures and is accessed by key.
A conflict rule that keeps the value with the latest timestamp, silently discarding the other write.
The key whose hash decides which node or partition stores an item, and which every efficient query must supply.
A graph model where nodes and relationships both have types and key-value properties.
Storing the id of a related document instead of the document itself, and fetching it separately.
A DynamoDB modelling style that stores several entity types in one table with generic key attributes so related items can be read together.
A 64-bit id whose high bits are a timestamp, so ids sort by creation time and can be generated without coordination.
In DynamoDB, the second part of a composite primary key; items in a partition are stored sorted by it and can be range-queried.
A deletion marker in Cassandra and other LSM stores; reads must skip it until compaction removes it.
An expiry time attached to a key or row, after which the store deletes it automatically.
A database organised as partitions of sorted rows with flexible columns, such as Cassandra, ScyllaDB or Bigtable.
drill:
Model: an LLM evaluation results store in DynamoDB

An ML platform team records evaluation results: each run evaluates one model on one dataset of 5,000 to 50,000 cases; each case result has a score, latency, token counts and a 2-20 KB output text. Access patterns: (P1) show a run's summary and its 100 worst-scoring cases; (P2) list runs for a model, newest first; (P3) compare one case's score across the last 10 runs of a model; (P4) fetch one case result's full output. About 200 runs a day; runs write results at up to 2,000 per second. Design the keys, indexes and item layout, and call out capacity risks.

Answer

Items. Run summary: PK = RUN#r1, SK = SUMMARY with model, dataset, started_at, aggregate scores. Case results: PK = RUN#r1, SK = CASE#c123 with score, latency and token counts, but not the output text; store outputs in S3 at a key derived from run and case (or as a separate item SK = OUT#c123) so the common reads stay small. P4 is then a GetItem plus an S3 fetch.

P1 worst cases. A sort key that orders by score within the run: add attributes GSI1PK = RUN#r1, GSI1SK = SCORE#0.1234#c123 (zero-padded so string order equals numeric order), and Query GSI1 ascending with Limit 100. The summary is a GetItem on the main key.

P2 runs per model. On the summary item, GSI2PK = MODEL#m7, GSI2SK = RUN#2026-10-03T12:00#r1; Query descending. Volume is small (200 runs a day across models), so no hot-partition risk.

P3 one case across runs. Add GSI3PK = MODEL#m7#CASE#c123, GSI3SK = started_at on case items, and Query the 10 newest. This index receives every case result write, so it doubles write cost; if P3 is rare, consider instead looking up the last 10 run ids via P2 and doing 10 GetItems.

Capacity risks. During a run, all 2,000 writes per second go to PK = RUN#r1, a single partition key value, which exceeds the 1,000 write units per second per-partition limit even for 1 KB items. Shard the run's case items: PK = RUN#r1#S{case_id mod 8}, and read the 8 shards in parallel for run-wide queries; GSI1's partition key needs the same treatment or the index throttles and back-pressures the table. Item sizes: keeping outputs out of the result items keeps writes at about 1 write unit each. Finally, analytics across runs (trends per dataset, per model) should come from a DynamoDB export to S3 queried by a warehouse engine, not from scans.
qa: E
Name the four main NoSQL data models and a typical use for each.

Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB used simply): sessions, caches, counters, rate limits. Document (MongoDB): aggregates such as user profiles, product catalogues, content with varying fields. Wide-column (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Bigtable): very high write volumes keyed by entity and time, such as messages, events, metrics. Graph (Neo4j, Neptune): relationship-heavy queries such as recommendations, fraud rings, permission inheritance.
E
When would you embed and when would you reference in a document database?

Embed data that belongs to the parent, is read with it, is bounded in size and is not shared, such as an order's line items or a user's addresses. Reference data that is shared by many parents, large or unbounded (a post's comments can grow without limit), updated independently, or queried on its own, such as products referenced from orders.
E
What is a partition key and why does it matter so much in Cassandra and DynamoDB?

It is the part of the key whose hash decides where an item lives. Efficient reads must supply it, all items with the same value sit together and can be range-read by the sort or clustering key, and all traffic for one value lands on one partition. Choosing it decides which queries are cheap, which are impossible, and whether load spreads evenly.
M
Design a Cassandra table for 'latest 50 messages in a channel' at Discord's scale.

Primary key ((channel_id, bucket), message_id) with message_id as a time-sortable id clustered in descending order. The partition key includes a time bucket, about 10 days in Discord's design, so even the busiest channels stay under roughly 100 MB per partition. A read computes the current bucket, reads the newest 50 rows from it, and walks back through earlier buckets if the channel is quiet.

Follow-up: Why not just (channel_id) as the partition key? — A channel can live for years, so its partition would grow without bound; very large partitions hurt compaction, repair and memory, and cannot be spread across nodes.
M
Explain DynamoDB single-table design with an example.

Store related entities in one table under generic keys: a user's profile at PK = USER#ana, SK = PROFILE, and their conversations at PK = USER#ana, SK = CONV#2026-10-03#c2. One Query on PK = USER#ana returns the profile and all conversations sorted by date, in one round trip, with no join. A GSI keyed on CONV#id supports the reverse lookup from conversation to owner. The cost is that the table is opaque to humans and analytics, and new access patterns may need new keys or GSIs and a backfill.
M
What is a hot partition and how do you avoid one in DynamoDB?

A single partition key value receiving too much traffic; each DynamoDB partition delivers at most 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second, so a viral item or a counter keyed by date saturates one partition however much table capacity you buy. Avoid it with high-cardinality partition keys, write sharding (append a random or computed suffix 0-9 and read all shards), caching hot reads, and spreading time-based writes across keys.
M
How do you model a many-to-many relationship in DynamoDB?

The adjacency-list pattern: store an item per edge in both directions, or one item per edge with a GSI that inverts the key. For students and courses, items PK = STUDENT#s1, SK = COURSE#c9 carry enrolment attributes, and a GSI with PK = COURSE#c9, SK = STUDENT#s1 answers 'students in a course'. Updates to shared attributes (a course title) must be propagated or kept only on the course item.
M
Why do Cassandra deletes and null writes cause performance problems?

Deletes and writes of null create tombstones, markers that must be replicated and that reads must skip until compaction removes them after gc_grace_seconds (10 days by default). Discord found that writing null for unset columns created 12 tombstones per message on average; queries that scan many tombstones slow down or fail. Write only non-null values and avoid queue-like delete-heavy patterns.
M
When is a graph database a better choice than SQL joins?

When queries traverse relationships of variable or large depth, such as 'accounts within four hops sharing a device or card', or shortest paths. A graph store follows stored adjacency pointers so cost grows with the edges actually visited; SQL needs a recursive query that joins whole tables per hop and is hard to plan well. For fixed one- or two-hop queries, indexed SQL joins are usually just as good and simpler to operate.
H
You are moving a MongoDB collection of posts with embedded comments to handle 10x growth. What breaks and how do you remodel?

Embedded comment arrays grow without bound: documents approach the 16 MB BSON limit, every new comment rewrites a large document, and reading a post drags all comments over the network. Move comments to their own collection keyed by post_id with an index on (post_id, created_at), keep a small denormalized summary in the post (comment count, latest three comments) updated on write, and paginate comments separately. That is the 'subset' pattern: embed the bounded, frequently read part, reference the rest.

Follow-up: How do you keep the comment count correct? — Update it atomically with $inc in the same write path as the insert, and run a periodic reconciliation that recounts, since the two writes are not in one transaction unless you use multi-document transactions.
H
Cassandra uses last-write-wins per column. Describe a bug this can cause and the fix.

Discord hit it: a user edited a message while another deleted it; because every write is an upsert, the edit recreated a row with only the edited column and the primary key, with author_id missing, and the application crashed on the null. Fixes: on read, treat rows missing a required column as deleted and clean them up (Discord's choice); avoid read-before-write assumptions; or use lightweight transactions (Paxos-based compare-and-set) for the rare operations that need them, at a high latency cost.
H
Design storage for an LLM chat product's conversations and messages in DynamoDB. Give keys, access patterns and pitfalls.

Access patterns: list a user's conversations newest first; load one conversation's messages in order; append a message; find a conversation by id. Keys: PK = USER#uid, SK = CONV#updated_ts#cid for the list (rewrite on update, or keep created time and sort client-side); PK = CONV#cid, SK = MSG#ts#mid for messages; a GSI on cid for direct lookup. Pitfalls: 400 KB item limit means large prompts or tool outputs go to S3 with a pointer; a long agent session can be a hot partition at 1,000 writes per second, so batch streaming tokens rather than writing each; and analytics need an export to S3 rather than scans.

Follow-up: What would you do differently in PostgreSQL? — conversations and messages tables with foreign keys and an index on (conversation_id, created_at); joins and ad-hoc analytics come free, and scale is ample unless you are at very large volume.
H
When would you recommend against NoSQL for a new product?

When access patterns are not yet known, which describes most new products: relational schemas absorb new queries with an index, while key-designed NoSQL tables need remodelling and backfills. Also when correctness depends on multi-entity transactions and constraints (payments, inventory), and when the team needs ad-hoc analytics. Choose NoSQL for a specific, known, high-scale access pattern (message timelines, session state, feature lookups) and keep the system of record relational unless scale forces otherwise.

Uniform activity across keys and the per-partition limit of 3,000 read and 1,000 write units per second.
AWS — Best practices for managing many-to-many relationships (adjacency lists)
Modelling graphs and many-to-many relationships in a key-value table with inverted indexes.
Embedding versus referencing, schema design patterns and validation.
The 16 MiB BSON document limit and other constraints that shape document design.
Query-driven modelling, partition and clustering keys, and the conceptual-to-physical process.

t: OLTP vs OLAP: columnar storage, data warehouses, and star and snowflake schemas
sum: Why analytical queries need a different engine from transactional ones: row versus column layout and the bytes each reads, run-length, dictionary and bit-packed encodings, zone maps, vectorised and late-materialised execution, Parquet, how warehouses are fed from OLTP systems, dimensional modelling with fact grain, star and snowflake schemas and slowly changing dimensions, and Google's Dremel turning hours into seconds.
prereq: db2
Normalization for OLTP; denormalization and materialized views for read paths; analytics flips the trade-off.
db5
Pages, B+ trees, LSM trees and write/read amplification; how a storage layout decides which operations are cheap.
db7
Scans, hash joins, hash aggregation and how the optimizer costs them.
sc8
OLTP versus OLAP and object storage at the system-design level.
why:
At Google in the mid-2000s, engineers analysing logs and crawl data had a frustrating loop. A question such as "how many web pages contain this kind of signal, grouped by language?" meant writing a MapReduce job, launching it on thousands of machines, and waiting hours, because every job read every byte of every record even when it needed two fields out of hundreds. In 2010 Google published the design of Dremel, a system it had run internally since 2006, which answered such questions interactively, aggregating over tables of a trillion rows in seconds. The paper's own comparison is the clearest demonstration of the idea at the heart of this lesson. On a table of 85 billion records, a MapReduce job reading records in their usual row-by-row format read 87 TB. The same job reading a columnar copy of the data, only the fields the query needed, read about 0.5 TB and went from hours to minutes. Dremel itself, which combined the columnar format with a tree of servers scanning in parallel, brought the same query down to seconds. Dremel became the engine behind BigQuery, and its columnar encoding of nested data inspired Apache Parquet.

The underlying problem is that two kinds of workload want opposite things from storage. A checkout service reads and writes individual rows: this order, this customer, this inventory item, thousands of times a second, each touching every column of a few rows. An analyst asks for total revenue by region by month over three years, touching two or three columns of hundreds of millions of rows, once. The first is OLTP (online transaction processing); everything in db1 to db11 has been about serving it well. The second is OLAP (online analytical processing), and serving it well needs a different layout (columns rather than rows), different compression, a different execution engine, a different schema style and, almost always, a different system fed from the first.

This lesson explains that second world from the bytes up. You will see why storing a table by column reduces the data a query reads by an order of magnitude or more, how columns compress so well, how analytical engines skip, vectorise and delay work, what Parquet files contain, how data flows from production databases into warehouses, and how to model a warehouse with facts, dimensions, star and snowflake schemas and history-preserving dimensions. The worked examples use a million-row sales table and an LLM usage warehouse, the kind of analytics every AI product needs for cost, latency and quality.
primer:
Filing by row versus filing by column

Imagine a company's sales records written on index cards, one card per sale, each card listing the date, region, product, quantity, price, customer and a note. Filed this way, by row, answering "what did sale 81,422 look like?" means pulling one card. But answering "what was total revenue last year?" means pulling every card, reading just two numbers from each, and putting it back. Most of the effort goes into handling the parts of the card you don't need.

Now file the same information differently: one long scroll for dates, another for regions, another for quantities, another for prices, all in the same order, so the 81,422nd entry on each scroll belongs to the same sale. That is filing by column. Total revenue now means unrolling only the quantity and price scrolls and multiplying entry by entry. The other five scrolls stay in the drawer. And the scrolls themselves become compressible: the region scroll says "north, north, south, north…" and can be written in a short code; the date scroll, if sales are filed in time order, says the same date thousands of times in a row and can be written as "day 100 × 3,000".

The analogy breaks where it should: looking up one complete sale now means visiting seven scrolls and finding the same position on each, and adding a new sale means appending to seven scrolls. Column layout makes whole-row operations expensive, which is why it is used for analysis, not for transaction processing.

Two systems, one pipeline

Because the layouts conflict, most organisations run two kinds of system. The production databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, DynamoDB) are row-oriented and serve the application. A data warehouse (BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift, ClickHouse, or an open-source engine such as DuckDB or Trino over Parquet files in a data lake) is column-oriented and serves analysts, dashboards and ML pipelines. Data flows from the first to the second continuously or in batches. And because analytics is about counting and slicing facts by their circumstances, warehouses use a schema style built for that, with a central table of facts surrounded by tables describing the who, what, where and when: the star schema. The rest of the lesson takes each piece in turn: layout, compression, execution, files, pipelines and modelling.

A sense of scale

It helps to put rough numbers on the two worlds. A busy OLTP database might handle 10,000 transactions a second, each reading or writing a handful of rows: tens of thousands of rows touched per second, each in a few milliseconds. A single analytical query over a year of that history touches hundreds of billions of row-values, once, and the user is happy to wait a few seconds. Reading 100 GB in five seconds needs 20 GB/s of throughput, which no single disk provides, but a cluster of machines each scanning its own compressed column slices does. That is why the analytical side is built around reading as little as possible, in parallel, and why the same hardware that runs one workload well runs the other badly.
body:
1. OLTP and OLAP, side by side

OLTPOLAP
Typical queryfetch or update one order by idrevenue by region by month over 3 years
Rows touched per query1 to hundredsmillions to billions
Columns touchedmost columns of those rowsa few columns of a wide table
Writesconstant small inserts and updatesbulk loads, appends; few updates
Concurrencythousands of short transactionstens of long queries
Latency targetmilliseconds per requestseconds to minutes per query
Schema stylenormalized (db2)dimensional, denormalized dimensions
Storage layoutrows in pages, B+ tree indexescompressed columns, zone maps

Every row of this table follows from the first two. When a query touches a few rows, the cost is finding them, so indexes matter and storing each row's values together makes the final fetch one page. When a query touches most rows, there is nothing to find; the cost is reading and processing bytes, so the winning moves are to read fewer bytes (only needed columns, compressed), skip blocks that cannot match, and process the remaining bytes as fast as the CPU allows.

2. Column storage and what a query reads

In a column store, each column of a table is stored separately, in the same row order, so the i-th value of every column belongs to row i. The lab builds a million-row sales table with seven columns. A revenue query needs two of them, qty and price. In row form, a disk-based engine reads every row (about 31 MiB at the lab's rough row width); in column form, it reads two 4-byte integer columns, 8 MiB, before any compression. Real warehouse tables are often 50 to 200 columns wide, and typical queries touch fewer than ten, so reading only the needed columns routinely cuts I/O by ten to fifty times. That is the first and biggest effect, and it is the one Dremel's 87 TB versus 0.5 TB comparison shows.

The costs are the mirror image. Reconstructing a full row means fetching the i-th value from every column, so "show me sale 81,422" touches as many files as there are columns. Inserting a row means appending to every column, and updating or deleting means rewriting or marking positions in each. Column stores therefore buffer writes: C-Store, the 2005 research system that became Vertica, paired a small write-optimised store with a large read-optimised column store and merged them in the background, and modern warehouses accept data in batches or micro-batches and write immutable compressed column segments, handling deletes with deletion vectors or tombstones that are compacted later, exactly the LSM idea (db5) applied to columns.

3. Encoding: why columns compress so well

A column holds values of one type, often with few distinct values or with order, so it compresses far better than rows that interleave dates, strings and numbers. Analytical engines use lightweight, type-aware encodings, chosen per column and often per block:

  • Run-length encoding (RLE) stores runs of repeated values as (value, count). The lab's day column, sorted by time with 3,000 sales per day, compresses from 1,000,000 values to 334 pairs, about 3,000 times fewer. Sorting a table by its most-filtered low-cardinality columns makes RLE effective on them.
  • Dictionary encoding replaces each value with a small integer code into a dictionary of distinct values. The lab's region column of four strings goes from about 4.3 MiB of text to 0.24 MiB of 2-bit codes. Comparisons like region = 'west' become integer comparisons on codes.
  • Bit-packing stores small integers in as few bits as their range needs: quantities 1-4 need 2 bits, not 32.
  • Delta encoding stores differences between consecutive values; increasing timestamps or ids become small deltas that then bit-pack well.

A general-purpose compressor such as Zstandard or Snappy is often applied on top. Typical analytical tables compress five to ten times overall; sorted, low-cardinality columns far more. Crucially, many operations run on encoded data directly. A SUM over an RLE column multiplies each run's value by its count; a filter on a dictionary-encoded column is evaluated once per distinct value and then becomes a lookup on codes; a COUNT DISTINCT on a dictionary column can count dictionary entries. So compression is not just storage savings; it is less work.

4. Skipping data: zone maps and partition pruning

The next best thing to reading fewer bytes is not reading blocks at all. Column stores and formats keep small statistics per block of each column, at least the minimum and maximum, often null counts and sometimes Bloom filters. These zone maps let a scan skip any block whose min-max range cannot satisfy the filter. A query on day BETWEEN 100 AND 130 over a table sorted by day reads only the blocks for those 31 days; the rest are eliminated from metadata alone. Zone maps are only as good as the data's order: on a column with random order, every block's range spans nearly everything and nothing is skipped. That is why warehouse tables are partitioned by date (whole partitions pruned by directory or metadata) and sorted or clustered within partitions by the next most common filters (tenant, region), the warehouse equivalent of choosing a clustered index (db6). BRIN indexes in PostgreSQL (db6) are the same idea inside a row store.

5. Execution: vectorised and late-materialised

Even after reading only the right bytes, a classic row-at-a-time engine (the iterator model of db7) spends most of its time on overhead: a function call per row per operator, type checks, branches. For billions of rows that overhead dominates. Vectorised execution, pioneered by the MonetDB/X100 research project and now used by DuckDB, ClickHouse, Snowflake and others, passes batches of values between operators, typically around 1,000 to 2,000 values of one column at a time. Each operator then runs a tight loop over a plain array (multiply these 1,024 quantities by these 1,024 prices), which the CPU executes with SIMD instructions, few branches and excellent cache behaviour. The difference is often ten times or more per core. (The lab's pure-Python loops cannot show this effect, since Python's own per-value overhead swamps the layout; the byte counts it prints are the part that transfers.)

Late materialisation delays building rows. To evaluate SELECT customer, price FROM sales WHERE region = 'west' AND day = 100, the engine scans the day column to produce the positions where day = 100, then reads the region column only at those positions to narrow further, and only then fetches customer and price for the surviving positions. Values that fail early filters are never decompressed or copied. Combined with zone maps, a selective analytical query may read a tiny fraction of even the columns it references.

Finally, analytical engines are massively parallel. Data is split into many chunks (files, row groups, partitions), each scanned and pre-aggregated by a separate thread or node, with partial results merged at the end, exactly Dremel's serving tree. Because analytical queries are scans and aggregations rather than coordinated transactions, they parallelise almost perfectly, which is how warehouses scale to petabytes.

6. Parquet and the data lake

Apache Parquet is the open columnar file format used across the data ecosystem. A Parquet file is divided into row groups (horizontal slices of rows, typically sized in the hundreds of megabytes); within each row group, each column is stored as a column chunk, divided into pages that carry encoded and compressed values. The file footer holds the schema and, for every column chunk, statistics such as min, max and null count, so a reader can open the footer, decide which row groups and columns it needs, and read only those byte ranges, the zone-map idea at file level. Parquet also encodes nested and repeated fields using Dremel's repetition and definition levels, so JSON-like records can be stored column by column.

Storing Parquet files in cheap object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob) and querying them with separate compute engines is the data lake architecture. Plain files lack transactions, schema evolution and efficient updates, so table formats (Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, Apache Hudi) add a metadata layer that tracks which files make up each version of a table, supporting atomic commits, time travel, partition evolution and row-level deletes. That combination is called a lakehouse. For an engineer, the practical upshot is that analytical data often lives as Parquet files plus table metadata, readable by many engines: Spark, Trino, DuckDB, Snowflake, BigQuery, and pandas or Polars in a notebook.

7. Getting data from OLTP into the warehouse

Warehouses are fed from operational systems, and the pipeline's design decides how fresh and how correct analytics are. The traditional approach is batch ETL (extract, transform, load): every night, extract changed rows from sources (using an updated_at column or a full dump), transform them into the warehouse schema, and load them. Modern warehouses are powerful enough that ELT is now common: load raw extracts first, then transform inside the warehouse with SQL (tools such as dbt manage those transformations as versioned code).

Batch extraction by timestamp misses deletes and can miss updates if timestamps are unreliable. Change data capture (CDC) reads the database's own log, PostgreSQL's logical decoding or MySQL's row-based binlog (db10), and emits every committed insert, update and delete in commit order, usually into a stream such as Kafka, from which they are landed in the lake or warehouse within seconds to minutes. CDC gives fresh, complete data without load on the source's tables, at the cost of operating the stream and handling schema changes. Whatever the mechanism, the loading step must be idempotent (replaying the same changes gives the same result, by merging on source primary key and change sequence) and reconciled (row counts and key totals compared with the source daily), because pipelines fail and restart.

Keeping analytics separate is not only about speed. Long analytical queries on a PostgreSQL primary hold old snapshots that block vacuum (db10), compete for buffer cache, and can be cancelled on standbys; a warehouse removes all of that coupling.

8. Dimensional modelling: facts, grain and dimensions

Warehouse schemas are designed differently from OLTP schemas, following the dimensional modelling approach associated with Ralph Kimball. The design starts from business processes (taking orders, shipping, serving an LLM request) and for each one asks: what is measured, and at what level of detail?

A fact table records the measurements of one process. Its first and most important design decision is the grain: exactly what one row represents, stated in business terms, such as "one row per order line" or "one row per LLM call". Every column must be true at that grain. Measures (facts) are usually numeric and additive: quantity, amount, tokens, cost, latency. Mixing grains is the classic error: putting an order-level shipping fee on every order-line row means anyone who sums it counts it once per line. Choose the most atomic grain the source provides; you can always aggregate up, never down.

A dimension table holds the descriptive context used to filter and group facts: date, product, customer, store, model, tenant. Dimensions are wide (dozens of attributes such as product name, brand, category, department, size, colour), relatively small (thousands to millions of rows, versus billions of facts) and deliberately denormalized: the category and department names sit directly on each product row. Each dimension row gets a surrogate key, an integer generated in the warehouse, independent of source-system ids, which lets the warehouse keep history (section 10) and merge entities from several sources. The fact table holds a foreign key to each dimension plus its measures. A date dimension, one row per calendar day with attributes such as weekday, week, month, quarter, fiscal period and holiday flags, is nearly universal, because "group by fiscal quarter" or "exclude holidays" then becomes a join and a filter rather than date arithmetic in every query.

9. Star and snowflake schemas

A fact table with its dimensions arranged around it forms a star schema: the fact at the centre, one join to each dimension. A typical query filters dimensions, joins to the fact, and aggregates measures:

SELECT d.month, p.category, s.region, SUM(f.amount) AS revenue
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_date d    ON d.date_key = f.date_key
JOIN dim_product p ON p.product_key = f.product_key
JOIN dim_store s   ON s.store_key = f.store_key
WHERE d.year = 2026 AND p.department = 'Electronics'
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3;

A snowflake schema normalizes dimensions further: product references a category table, which references a department table. It removes repeated names and can make shared hierarchies easier to maintain, but it adds joins to every query and complicates the SQL that analysts and BI tools generate. Because dimensions are small relative to facts, the redundancy a star keeps costs little, and most practitioners prefer stars, snowflaking only very large or shared sub-dimensions. Columnar engines also reduce the cost of wide denormalized tables, since unused columns are never read, which is why some teams go further and build fully flattened "one big table" models for specific dashboards.

When several fact tables share dimensions with the same keys and meanings (the same dim_date, dim_customer and dim_product for orders, shipments and returns), the dimensions are called conformed, and results from different processes can be combined reliably, for example return rate by product category, which divides one fact's aggregate by another's at the same dimensional grain.

10. Slowly changing dimensions

Dimension attributes change: a customer moves city, a product changes category, a tenant upgrades plan, a model's price per million tokens changes. The question is whether old facts should be reported under the old or the new value. Slowly changing dimension (SCD) techniques answer it. Type 1 overwrites the attribute in place: simple, no history; appropriate for corrections and for attributes whose history nobody needs. Type 2 preserves history: when the attribute changes, the current dimension row is closed (valid_to set, is_current false) and a new row is inserted with a new surrogate key, the new value and valid_from = now. New facts get the new surrogate key; old facts keep pointing to the old row. Now "revenue by customer city at the time of sale" is correct, and "revenue by customer's current city" is a join to the current row by the durable source id.

Type 2 is why warehouses use surrogate keys rather than source ids: the same source customer id corresponds to several dimension rows over time. The loading step must look up the dimension row valid at each fact's event time, an as-of join, not the current one. For an LLM cost warehouse, the model dimension is a natural type 2 candidate: if prices change on 1 March, calls before and after must be costed at their own prices, and a type 1 overwrite would silently revalue history.

11. Pre-aggregation: rollups, materialized views and cubes

Even a fast columnar scan of billions of rows costs seconds and money, and dashboards ask the same questions repeatedly. Warehouses therefore precompute. A rollup or aggregate table stores the fact table summarised at a coarser grain, for example revenue and units by day, product category and region instead of by order line. If the base fact has 2 billion rows and the rollup 3 million, every dashboard query against the rollup reads a thousandth of the data. The rollup must be maintained: rebuilt on a schedule, or incrementally updated for the most recent partitions, the same derived-copy discipline as db2's denormalization, with the base fact as the source of truth and a reconciliation check that rollup totals equal base totals.

Materialized views automate this inside the engine: the warehouse stores a query's result and keeps it up to date, and some engines (BigQuery, Snowflake, ClickHouse's materialized views and aggregating tables) can rewrite a query against the base table to read the view automatically when it answers the question. Classic OLAP cubes took the idea to its limit, precomputing aggregates for every combination of dimensions (a GROUP BY CUBE, db3) so any slice was a lookup; they are fast but grow exponentially with the number of dimensions, which is why modern columnar engines mostly replaced them with fast scans plus a few targeted rollups.

Some measures cannot be rolled up naively. Sums and counts add across groups, but averages must be stored as sum and count, distinct counts cannot be added (users active on Monday plus users active on Tuesday double-counts people active on both), and percentiles cannot be combined at all. Approximate sketches solve the distinct and percentile cases: HyperLogLog sketches can be merged to estimate distinct counts across groups, and t-digest or similar sketches can be merged to estimate latency percentiles. A rollup of LLM calls by day and model that stores token sums, call counts, a HyperLogLog of user ids and a latency sketch can answer cost, volume, distinct users and p95 latency for any date range by merging stored values.

12. A worked design: LLM usage analytics

Pull the lesson together on the warehouse an AI platform needs. The process is serving LLM calls; the grain is one row per call. The fact table fact_llm_call carries surrogate keys to dim_date, dim_tenant (type 2: plan and region change), dim_user, dim_model (type 2: provider, context window and price per million input and output tokens) and dim_prompt_version (prompt hash, template name, author, release date), plus measures: input tokens, output tokens, cost (computed at load time from the model row valid at the call's time), latency, status and cache-hit flag. A second fact table at the grain of one evaluation result shares dim_model and dim_prompt_version, so cost and quality can be compared per prompt version, a conformed-dimension join.

Physical design follows the access patterns: partition fact_llm_call by date (old partitions are cheap to drop or archive), cluster or sort by tenant within partitions so per-tenant dashboards skip most blocks, store it as Parquet or in a columnar warehouse, and feed it from the application's call log via CDC so dashboards are minutes behind production. The questions finance and product ask, cost per tenant per model per day, p95 latency by model and region, error rate after a prompt release, quality versus cost per prompt version, all become "filter dimensions, group by dimensions, aggregate measures" over columns that compress extremely well (dates, model keys and statuses run-length or dictionary encode to almost nothing).
deep:
Dremel's nested columnar encoding

Flat relational tables are straightforward to store by column. Google's data, however, was nested: protocol-buffer records with repeated and optional fields, such as a document with several links, each with several languages. Dremel's contribution was a lossless columnar representation of such records.
