For each field path, it stores the values in a column together with two small integers per value: a repetition level, which says at which nesting level a repeated field started repeating (so the reader knows whether a value starts a new record, a new parent element, or continues a list), and a definition level, which says how many of the optional or repeated fields on the path were actually present (so missing values at different depths can be told apart). With these, a query reading only Links.Forward reads one column and can still reconstruct which record and which link each value belonged to. Parquet adopted the same scheme. The paper also measured where columnar storage stops paying off: reading time grows with the number of fields, and the crossover with record-oriented storage often lay at dozens of fields, which is why columnar formats suit analytical queries that touch a small subset of a wide record.

Why vectorisation beats tuple-at-a-time

The iterator model calls next() on each operator for each row, so for a simple filter-and-sum over a billion rows the engine makes billions of virtual function calls, each with branching on types and NULLs. Modern CPUs execute simple arithmetic in a fraction of a nanosecond but pay many nanoseconds for mispredicted branches and cache misses. Vectorised engines amortise the per-call overhead over a vector of values and write each operator as a loop over primitive arrays with no per-value type dispatch, which compilers turn into SIMD instructions processing 4 to 16 values per instruction. The vector size is chosen to keep the working set in the CPU's L1 or L2 cache (around a thousand values). An alternative, used by HyPer and Umbra, is to compile each query into machine code that fuses operators into tight loops ("data-centric code generation"). Both approaches reach similar speeds and both are far faster than tuple-at-a-time interpretation; DuckDB, ClickHouse, Velox and DataFusion are vectorised, while several commercial systems combine both techniques.

Joins in a star schema

Star-schema queries have a characteristic shape: one huge fact table joined to several small, filtered dimensions. Engines exploit it. Each filtered dimension is small enough to build a hash table on (db7), so the fact table is scanned once and probed against each dimension's hash table in a pipeline. Better, the dimension filters can be pushed into the fact scan before the join: build a Bloom filter or a set of qualifying dimension keys from each filtered dimension and use it to skip fact rows, or, with zone maps, whole fact blocks, before any join work. This is sometimes called a semi-join reduction or runtime filter, and it means a query for one department and one month reads a small fraction of the fact table even though the filter was written on dimensions. Classic data warehouses called the same idea a star join or star transformation.

HTAP and the convergence of OLTP and OLAP

Running two systems with a pipeline between them adds latency and operational cost, so there is steady effort to serve both workloads from one system, called HTAP (hybrid transactional/analytical processing). Approaches include keeping a row store for transactions plus an in-memory column copy for analytics, kept in sync automatically (Oracle's in-memory column store, SQL Server columnstore indexes, SAP HANA); a row store replicated to a columnar replica (TiDB's TiFlash, AlloyDB's columnar engine); and columnar extensions for PostgreSQL. They work well for moderate scales and for "operational analytics" over fresh data. At large scale most organisations still separate the workloads, because isolation of resources and failure domains, different retention policies, and data from many sources favour a dedicated warehouse or lakehouse.

Inmon, Kimball and the data vault

There are competing philosophies of warehouse architecture. Kimball's dimensional approach builds star schemas per business process, tied together by conformed dimensions, and is optimised for query simplicity. Inmon's corporate information factory builds a normalized, enterprise-wide integrated warehouse first and derives dimensional data marts from it, favouring integration and consistency. The data vault methodology models hubs (business keys), links (relationships) and satellites (time-stamped attributes), insert-only, optimised for auditability and for loading from many changing sources, and is then typically projected into star schemas for consumption. Modern ELT practice often mixes them: raw landed data, a cleaned and integrated layer, and dimensional or wide "mart" tables for consumption, sometimes described as bronze, silver and gold layers in lakehouse terminology.
prod:
Dremel's numbers, and what they mean for your warehouse

Dremel's evaluation, on system instances running in shared data centres alongside other applications, makes the columnar argument with real workloads. On a table of 85 billion records using 3,000 nodes, a MapReduce job over record-oriented storage read 87 TB; the same job over columnar storage read about 0.5 TB and dropped from hours to minutes; Dremel, adding its serving tree and interactive design, answered in seconds. The paper reports that in a typical month most queries finished in under 10 seconds and some scanned close to 100 billion records per second. The lesson for any warehouse is the ordering of the levers: first read fewer bytes (columns, compression, pruning), then parallelise. A warehouse bill or a slow dashboard almost always traces to bytes scanned, which is why cloud warehouses such as BigQuery bill by bytes processed and why partitioning and clustering choices are cost decisions.

Common warehouse failures

Grain errors produce double-counting that looks plausible: a header-level amount repeated on line-level rows, or a join to a dimension that is accidentally not unique (two current rows for one customer after a buggy type 2 load), which fans out facts exactly like the db3 fan-out bug. Defences are uniqueness tests on dimension keys and current flags, and reconciliation of fact totals against source totals. Late-arriving data: events that arrive hours after their event time land in already-aggregated partitions, so pipelines must reprocess recent partitions or merge late rows. Schema drift: a source column renamed or retyped silently breaks transformations; CDC pipelines need schema-change handling and alerts. Small files: streaming ingestion that writes thousands of tiny Parquet files per hour destroys scan efficiency, since each file has fixed overhead; table formats provide compaction jobs to merge them. Unbounded costs: an analyst's SELECT * over a multi-terabyte table in a bytes-billed warehouse is a real bill, so require partition filters on large tables and set per-user quotas.

Data quality and contracts

Because warehouses aggregate data from many producers, quality problems compound. Teams increasingly treat important tables as products with data contracts: declared schemas, freshness targets (for example, yesterday's data complete by 06:00), and tests (non-null keys, unique keys, accepted values, referential integrity between facts and dimensions, row-count bounds) run on every load by tools such as dbt tests or Great Expectations. Failing tests block publication of downstream tables rather than letting a dashboard silently show a wrong number. For ML, the same tables feed training sets, so a silent quality regression becomes a model regression; point-in-time correctness (training features joined as of the label's time, the as-of join of type 2 dimensions) is the warehouse discipline that prevents leakage (hd8).

Analytics for AI products

AI products generate analytical data at high volume: every model call, retrieval, tool invocation, user rating and evaluation result. Three practical recommendations follow from this lesson. Log calls in the OLTP or logging path with stable ids and timestamps, and get them into a columnar store quickly via CDC or a stream, rather than running analytics on the production database. Model them dimensionally, with model and prompt versions as type 2 dimensions so cost and quality history stays correct when prices change or prompts are revised. And keep large payloads (prompts, completions, retrieved documents) out of the fact table: store them in object storage or a separate table keyed by call id, because columnar engines handle wide text columns poorly and most analytical queries never need them. Done this way, questions like "did the new prompt version reduce cost per resolved conversation for enterprise tenants without hurting ratings?" become a single star-schema query that runs in seconds.
myths: A data warehouse is just a bigger database.

It is built for a different workload: few, large queries that scan and aggregate millions or billions of rows over a handful of columns, with data loaded in bulk. That workload rewards columnar storage, heavy compression, massive parallel scans and denormalized dimensional schemas, all of which would be poor choices for an OLTP system doing thousands of single-row reads and writes per second.
Columnar databases are faster for everything.

They are faster when a query touches a few columns of many rows. Fetching or updating one whole row means touching every column file, so point lookups and single-row updates are slow, which is why columnar stores batch writes and are rarely used as the system of record for transactions.
Star schemas are bad design because they are denormalized.

Dimension tables in a star schema are deliberately denormalized (category and department names repeated on each product row) because they are small, rarely updated and joined to huge fact tables in every query. The fact table itself is normalized to its grain. Analytics reads in aggregate and loads in bulk, so redundancy in small dimensions costs little and saves joins.
You can run analytics on the production OLTP database if you add indexes.

Indexes help selective queries; analytical queries are unselective by nature, scanning most of a table, so they compete with production traffic for I/O, CPU, memory and locks, hold old snapshots that block vacuum, and are slow on row storage anyway. A replica helps with isolation but not with layout; a warehouse or columnar engine fed by change data capture is the standard answer.
Compression is a storage saving that costs CPU at query time.

In columnar engines compression usually makes queries faster: fewer bytes are read from disk or memory, and many operations (comparisons on dictionary codes, sums over run-length runs) run directly on compressed data without decompressing every value.
lab:
Goal: measure the bytes a row layout and a column layout must read for the same query, see how much run-length and dictionary encoding shrink real-looking columns, and run a star-schema query. Python 3.12 standard library (SQLite itself is a row store; it stands in for the warehouse only to show the query shape). Save as db12.py; it builds a million rows, so allow a few seconds.

import array, random, sqlite3, time

random.seed(12)
N = 1_000_000
regions = ["north", "south", "east", "west"]
# one fact table: (day, region, product_id, qty, price_cents, customer_id, note)
rows = [(i // 3_000, random.choice(regions), random.randrange(500), random.randrange(1, 5),
         random.randrange(100, 10_000), random.randrange(100_000), "promo" if i % 10 == 0 else "")
        for i in range(N)]

# Row layout: each query walks whole rows. Column layout: one array per column.
cols = {"qty": array.array("i", (r[3] for r in rows)),
        "price": array.array("i", (r[4] for r in rows))}

s1 = sum(r[3] * r[4] for r in rows)
s2 = sum(q * p for q, p in zip(cols["qty"], cols["price"]))
assert s1 == s2                          # same answer; what differs is what must be read
row_bytes = N * (4 * 6 + 8)              # rough: six 4-byte numbers/codes + a short string
col_bytes = 2 * 4 * N                    # only the two columns the query needs
print(f"bytes a disk-based engine must read: rows ~{row_bytes/2**20:.0f} MiB vs columns {col_bytes/2**20:.0f} MiB")

# Compression that columns make possible
day_col = [r[0] for r in rows]                         # sorted by time: long runs
runs = 1 + sum(1 for a, b in zip(day_col, day_col[1:]) if a != b)
print(f"day column: {N:,} values -> {runs} run-length pairs ({N/runs:,.0f}x fewer)")
region_codes = {r: i for i, r in enumerate(regions)}   # dictionary encoding: 2 bits/value
print(f"region column: text ~{sum(len(r[1]) for r in rows)/2**20:.1f} MiB -> dictionary codes {N*2/8/2**20:.2f} MiB")

# A star schema query in SQLite
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE dim_product (product_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, category TEXT);
CREATE TABLE fact_sales (day INT, region TEXT, product_id INT, qty INT, price_cents INT);
""")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO dim_product VALUES (?, ?)", [(p, ["books", "games", "music"][p % 3]) for p in range(500)])
db.executemany("INSERT INTO fact_sales VALUES (?,?,?,?,?)", (r[:5] for r in rows))
q = """SELECT p.category, f.region, SUM(f.qty * f.price_cents) / 100 AS revenue
       FROM fact_sales f JOIN dim_product p USING (product_id)
       WHERE f.day BETWEEN 100 AND 130 GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY revenue DESC LIMIT 3"""
t0 = time.perf_counter(); top = db.execute(q).fetchall()
print(f"star query (top category/region, days 100-130): {top}  {1000*(time.perf_counter()-t0):.0f} ms")

What to look for.

  1. About 31 MiB must be read in row form for a revenue query versus 8 MiB for the two needed columns, before compression: the column-pruning effect alone is about 4x here, and grows with table width.
  2. The time-sorted day column collapses from 1,000,000 values to 334 run-length pairs, about 3,000x; the four-value region column shrinks from about 4.3 MiB of text to 0.24 MiB of 2-bit dictionary codes.
  3. The star query returns the top three category-region pairs by revenue for days 100-130. In a columnar engine it would read the day, region, product and two measure columns, skip every block outside days 100-130 using zone maps, and join to the 500-row product dimension through a small hash table.

Try next. Shuffle the rows before computing the day runs (random.shuffle(rows)) and watch RLE collapse to nearly one run per value: order is what makes RLE and zone maps work. If you can install DuckDB in a virtual environment of your own (it is not installed here), write the table to Parquet and run the same query with EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see vectorised scans and filter pushdown.
recap: OLTP workloads run many short transactions that read and write a few rows by key; OLAP workloads run fewer large queries that scan, join and aggregate many rows over a few columns.
Row storage keeps each row's values together, ideal for reading or writing whole rows; column storage keeps each column's values together, so a query reads only the columns it uses.
Columns of one type compress well: run-length encoding for sorted or repetitive values, dictionary encoding for low-cardinality strings, and bit-packing and delta encoding for integers.
Columnar engines skip data with min/max zone maps, execute on batches of values (vectorised execution) and assemble rows only for qualifying positions (late materialisation).
Parquet stores data in row groups split into column chunks with statistics, and is the common file format of data lakes and lakehouse table formats.
Warehouses are fed from OLTP systems by batch ETL/ELT or by change data capture streams, and are kept separate so analytics cannot hurt production.

Dimensional modelling starts by declaring the grain of the fact table, then attaches dimension tables of descriptive attributes; a star schema has denormalized dimensions, a snowflake schema normalizes them.
Slowly changing dimensions record how dimension attributes change over time; type 1 overwrites and type 2 adds a new row with validity dates.
Google's Dremel showed the effect of columnar storage at scale: a query over 85 billion records read 0.5 TB in columnar form versus 87 TB for record-oriented MapReduce, going from hours to seconds.
glossary: A database or file format that stores each column's values contiguously rather than each row's values.
A dimension table shared with the same meaning and keys across several fact tables, so their results can be combined.
Cheap object storage holding raw and processed data files, often Parquet, queried by separate engines.
Storing the differences between consecutive values instead of the values, effective for sorted numbers and timestamps.
Replacing repeated values with small integer codes plus a lookup table of distinct values.
A table of descriptive attributes (product, customer, date) used to filter and group facts.
Extract-load-transform or extract-transform-load: moving data from sources into a warehouse and reshaping it, before or after loading.
A table of measurements at a declared grain, such as one row per order line, with foreign keys to dimensions.
Exactly what one row of a fact table represents.
Hybrid transactional/analytical processing: serving OLTP and OLAP workloads from one system.
A small mergeable sketch that estimates the number of distinct values in a set.
An architecture that adds table formats (Iceberg, Delta Lake, Hudi) with transactions and schema evolution on top of files in a data lake.
Working on column positions and values for as long as possible and assembling full rows only for the final qualifying positions.
Massively parallel processing: spreading a query across many nodes that each scan and aggregate their own data slice.
Online analytical processing: large scanning and aggregating queries over historical data.
Online transaction processing: many short reads and writes of individual rows.
An open columnar file format with row groups, column chunks, encodings and per-chunk statistics.
A pre-aggregated copy of a fact table at a coarser grain, used to answer common queries cheaply.
Storing a run of identical consecutive values as (value, count).
Single instruction, multiple data: CPU instructions that apply one operation to several values at once.
A technique for handling changes to dimension attributes over time; type 2 keeps history by adding versioned rows.
A dimensional model whose dimension tables are normalized into further tables, such as product to category to department.
A dimensional model with one central fact table joined to denormalized dimension tables.
An integer key generated in the warehouse for each dimension row, independent of source-system ids.
Processing a batch of values (for example 1,024) per operator call in tight loops, instead of one row at a time.
Per-block minimum and maximum values that let a scan skip blocks that cannot match a filter.
drill:
Design: from an OLTP schema to a warehouse

An e-commerce PostgreSQL database has orders(order_id, customer_id, created_at, shipping_fee, status), order_lines(order_id, line_no, product_id, qty, unit_price), products(product_id, name, category_id), categories(category_id, name, department) and customers(customer_id, name, city, segment). Analysts want revenue and units by day, category, department, customer segment and city, with city as it was at the time of the order, plus average shipping fee per order by segment. Design the warehouse model, the load process, and point out the trap in the shipping fee.

Answer

Grain. The main process is selling products, so the fact table fact_order_line is one row per order line: keys to dim_date (order date), dim_product, dim_customer; degenerate dimension order_id (kept on the fact for counting distinct orders); measures qty, revenue = qty * unit_price.

Dimensions. dim_product as a star: product name, category name and department flattened onto each product row (snowflaking categories would add a join for little benefit). dim_customer as SCD type 2 on city and segment: surrogate key, source customer_id, attributes, valid_from, valid_to, is_current. dim_date with day, week, month, quarter, holiday flags.

The trap. Shipping fee is an order-level fact. Putting it on every order-line row means SUM(shipping_fee) counts it once per line. Either create a second fact table at order grain, fact_order(order_key, date_key, customer_key, shipping_fee, line_count), conformed on the same dimensions, or allocate the fee across lines (by revenue share) if a line-level number is truly needed and everyone agrees on the rule. Average fee per order by segment then comes from fact_order.

Load. CDC from PostgreSQL logical decoding into the lake; customer changes processed first into dim_customer (close the current row, insert the new one); order lines looked up against the customer row valid at orders.created_at (an as-of join), not the current row, so city-at-time-of-order is correct. Merges keyed on (order_id, line_no) make reloads idempotent; status changes (cancellations) handled either as updates in a mutable recent window or as negative adjustment rows. Physical: partition both facts by order date, cluster by customer segment; daily reconciliation of revenue and line counts against the source.
qa: E
What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP workloads?

OLTP runs many short transactions, each reading or writing a few rows by key, with strict latency and concurrency needs: placing an order, updating a profile. OLAP runs fewer, much larger queries that scan and aggregate large fractions of the data over a few columns: revenue by region by month. They want opposite storage layouts and are usually served by different systems.
E
Why is columnar storage faster for analytics?

An analytical query usually reads a few of many columns. Column storage reads only those columns' data, so a query using 3 of 50 columns reads roughly 6% of the bytes. Each column holds one type with similar values, so it compresses much better, and engines process columns in tight loops over batches, which uses CPU caches and SIMD instructions efficiently.
E
What is a star schema?

A central fact table holding measurements at a declared grain (for example one row per order line, with quantity and amount) and foreign keys to surrounding dimension tables (date, product, customer, store) that hold descriptive attributes. Queries filter and group on dimension attributes and aggregate fact measures, with one join per dimension.
M
Explain run-length, dictionary and delta encoding with an example of each.

Run-length: a date column sorted by time, with 3,000 rows per day, becomes one (day, 3000) pair per day; the lab's million-row column collapsed to 334 pairs. Dictionary: a region column with four distinct strings becomes 2-bit codes plus a 4-entry dictionary, about 18x smaller than the text. Delta: increasing timestamps 1700000000, 1700000003, 1700000007 become a base plus small differences 3 and 4 that need only a few bits each.
M
What is the grain of a fact table and why decide it first?

The grain states exactly what one fact row represents, such as one row per order line per day. Every measure and dimension must be true at that grain; mixing grains (order-level shipping cost on order-line rows) leads to double counting when users sum. Declaring the most atomic practical grain keeps the table flexible, since it can always be aggregated up but never broken down.
M
What is a slowly changing dimension type 2 and when do you need it?

When a dimension attribute changes, such as a customer moving from Pune to Mumbai, type 2 closes the current row (valid_to = now, is_current = false) and inserts a new row with a new surrogate key and the new value. Facts recorded before the move keep pointing to the old row, so 'revenue by customer city at time of sale' stays historically correct. Type 1 simply overwrites, which is fine when history does not matter.
M
Why shouldn't analysts query the production PostgreSQL primary directly?

Analytical queries scan large tables and compete with production traffic for CPU, I/O and buffer cache; long queries hold old snapshots that stop vacuum (db10); and row storage makes them slow anyway. Use a replica for light ad-hoc reads at most, and move serious analytics to a columnar warehouse fed by CDC or batch loads.
M
Star versus snowflake schema: what are the trade-offs?

A star keeps each dimension as one wide denormalized table, so queries need one join per dimension and are simple to write and fast; dimension attributes are repeated. A snowflake normalizes dimensions into sub-dimensions (product to category to department), saving a little space and making some hierarchies cleaner, at the cost of more joins and more complex queries. Since dimensions are small relative to facts, stars are usually preferred.
M
What are zone maps and how do they help?

Columnar engines and file formats store the minimum and maximum of each column for each block or row group. A filter like day BETWEEN 100 AND 130 can skip any block whose range does not overlap, without reading it. They work best when data is sorted or clustered by the filtered column, which is why tables are often sorted or partitioned by time.
H
Explain vectorised execution and late materialisation.

Vectorised engines pass batches of values (say 1,024) between operators instead of one row at a time, so each operator runs a tight loop over a column array, amortising interpretation overhead and using SIMD and caches. Late materialisation keeps working on column positions: evaluate the filter on one column to get a selection of positions, fetch the next column only at those positions, and assemble full rows only for the final result, avoiding decompressing and copying values that will be discarded.
H
Dremel queried trillion-row tables in seconds. What design choices made that possible?

A columnar format for nested records (repetition and definition levels), so queries read only the fields they reference: in the paper's experiment over 85 billion records, about 0.5 TB of columnar data versus 87 TB for record-oriented MapReduce. Plus a multi-level serving tree that fans a query out to thousands of leaf servers scanning in parallel and aggregates partial results on the way up, and tolerance of stragglers. The design became BigQuery and inspired Parquet's nested encoding.
Follow-up: When does record-oriented storage win? — The paper found the crossover at dozens of fields read; queries that need most fields of each record, or single-record lookups, favour row layout.
H
Design the pipeline that gets OLTP data into a warehouse with low latency and correct history.

Capture changes from the OLTP database's log with CDC (logical decoding or binlog), publish them to a stream, land raw change events in the lake or warehouse, then transform into dimension and fact tables: dimensions merged with SCD type 2 logic keyed on source ids, facts appended at their grain with surrogate dimension keys looked up by event time. Use idempotent merges keyed on source primary key and change sequence so replays are safe, and reconcile row counts and sums against the source daily.
H
Model a warehouse for LLM usage analytics: cost per tenant per model per day, latency percentiles, and quality scores by prompt version.

Fact table at the grain of one LLM call: date key, time, tenant key, user key, model key, prompt-version key, input and output tokens, cost, latency, status, and an optional quality score. Dimensions: date, tenant (SCD type 2 for plan changes), model (with provider and price list, type 2 since prices change), prompt version (text hash, author, release date). Partition the fact by date and cluster by tenant. A second fact table at the grain of one evaluation result links to the same model and prompt-version dimensions so quality and cost can be compared.
refs: Melnik et al. — Dremel: Interactive Analysis of Web-Scale Datasets (VLDB 2010)
Columnar storage for nested data and serving trees: 85 billion records, 0.5 TB columnar versus 87 TB record-oriented, hours to seconds.
Stonebraker et al. — C-Store: A Column-oriented DBMS (VLDB 2005)
The column-store research system behind Vertica: projections, compression and a read-optimised store.
Row groups, column chunks, pages, encodings and statistics.
Kimball Group — Star Schemas and OLAP Cubes
Dimensional modelling from its main proponents: facts, dimensions and star schemas.
An embeddable vectorised columnar engine you can run locally on Parquet files.

t: Using databases from applications: connection pooling, ORMs, N+1 queries and pagination
sum: Where application code meets the database: what a connection costs, sizing pools with Little's law and why small pools win, PgBouncer's pool modes, transactions and timeouts in request code, how ORMs generate SQL, counting and fixing N+1 queries, OFFSET versus keyset pagination worked on a million rows, bulk writes, prepared statements and retries.
prereq: db7
Query plans, nested loops versus hash joins, and how the planner uses indexes.
db9
Transactions, row locks, deadlocks and retrying serialization failures.
db10
PostgreSQL's process-per-connection model and PgBouncer; idle-in-transaction sessions hold back vacuum.
db6
Composite indexes serve WHERE plus ORDER BY; the leftmost-prefix rule.
why:
The HikariCP project, maintainers of one of the most widely used Java connection pools, keeps a short wiki page called "About Pool Sizing" that begins with a scenario: a website with 10,000 users making database requests simultaneously, about 20,000 transactions per second. How big should the connection pool be? Most engineers' instinct is "big": thousands of connections, one per concurrent user, or at least hundreds. The page points to a demonstration by Oracle's Real-World Performance group in which a system's pool was cut from 2,048 connections to 96, with no other change, and response times fell from about 100 milliseconds to about 2: fifty times faster with twenty times fewer connections. Its conclusion is that even 96 was probably too many unless the database had 16 or 32 cores.

That counter-intuitive result is typical of the boundary between application code and the database, which is where a large share of real-world database performance problems actually live. The database itself may be well designed, normalized, indexed and tuned, and the application can still make it slow by opening too many connections, by asking for data one row at a time in a loop, by paginating in a way that gets slower on every page, by holding transactions open while it waits for something else, or by retrying writes in a way that duplicates them. None of these are visible in the schema. They are visible in how the application talks to the database.

Many of them come from abstractions that are genuinely useful. Object-relational mappers (ORMs) let developers work with objects rather than SQL strings, and their lazy loading, which fetches related data only when you touch it, makes code simple. It also makes it easy to write a loop that sends one query per item. GitLab's development guidelines take this seriously enough to enforce a budget: each controller, API endpoint or background worker may run at most 100 SQL queries, and the test suite raises an error when one exceeds it.

This lesson works through the application side of the database. It explains what a connection costs and how to size pools with a simple law from queueing theory, how poolers such as PgBouncer multiplex connections and what they break, how ORMs turn code into SQL and how to count and fix N+1 queries, why OFFSET pagination degrades and how keyset pagination fixes it, and the habits that keep transactions short and retries safe. The lab measures N+1 and OFFSET on a million rows. Throughout, the examples include LLM-backed services, which add a new hazard: requests that spend seconds waiting on a model while holding database resources.
primer:
The database is a shared, remote, limited resource

From inside application code, a database call looks like a function call: post.author.name, Order.objects.filter(...). That illusion is the source of most problems. Three facts break it.

First, the database is remote. Every query is a round trip over the network: serialise the request, send it, wait for the database to parse, plan and execute it, receive the result. Even inside one data centre, a round trip costs roughly a few hundred microseconds to a millisecond before the query does any work. A function call costs nanoseconds. Code that makes a hundred small database calls where one would do pays the round trip a hundred times.

Second, the database is shared. Every application instance, worker and analyst talks to the same server. Connections, locks, memory and CPU are shared among all of them, so one request's habits (holding a transaction open, scanning a large table) affect everyone else's latency.

Third, the database is limited. It can only execute as many queries truly in parallel as it has CPU cores and I/O capacity. Ask it to run more at once, and it does not get more done; it time-slices between them, adding overhead, while they contend for the same locks and buffers.

A restaurant kitchen

Think of the database as a restaurant kitchen with eight cooks (cores), and of connections as order tickets on the rail. If waiters put 8 or 16 tickets on the rail, cooks work steadily and food comes out fast. If waiters put 2,000 tickets up because there are 2,000 diners, the cooks do not cook faster; they spend their time reading tickets, switching between dishes and bumping into each other at the stove, and every dish takes longer. The right design is for waiters to hold orders at the front (the connection pool's queue) and feed the kitchen only as fast as it can cook. That is the pool-sizing result in one picture.

The analogy also covers the other topics. A waiter who goes to the kitchen once per ingredient instead of once per order is the N+1 problem. A waiter who keeps a ticket on the rail while chatting with a table, so the cooks keep the station reserved, is a transaction held open across a slow external call. And a waiter asked for "the 9,001st order of the day" who counts through the first 9,000 tickets each time is OFFSET pagination.

What this lesson gives you

Each section below turns one of those habits into a rule you can check in code review. How many connections can this service open in total, and is that a small multiple of the database's cores? Where does each transaction start and end, and does anything slow happen in between? How many queries does this endpoint run, and does the number grow with the size of the list it renders? How does this list paginate, and what happens on page 10,000? If this write is retried, can it happen twice? None of these questions needs database internals to answer, only an honest look at what the application actually sends.
body:
1. What a connection costs

Opening a connection to PostgreSQL involves a TCP handshake, usually a TLS handshake, authentication (with SCRAM, several messages), and on the server, forking a new backend process that allocates its own memory and builds caches of catalog information as queries run. Altogether that is commonly a few milliseconds, sometimes tens of milliseconds over TLS across zones, compared with sub-millisecond simple queries. MySQL's thread-per-connection model is cheaper per connection, but the handshake and authentication costs remain. And every open connection consumes server memory whether or not it is busy: a PostgreSQL backend that has run a few queries can easily hold several megabytes, and more if queries used large work_mem sorts.

So the first rule is to reuse connections. A connection pool keeps a set of open connections and lends one to each unit of work: the application borrows a connection, runs its transaction, and returns it. Most frameworks provide one (SQLAlchemy's engine pool, HikariCP for Java, the pools in Go's database/sql and in Node drivers). The pool also acts as a limiter: when all connections are lent out, further requests wait in the pool's queue for one to come back, up to a timeout, which protects the database from overload.

2. Sizing the pool with Little's law

Little's law says that in any stable system, the average number of items inside equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends inside: L = λW. Apply it to connections. If a service runs 2,000 transactions per second and each holds a connection for 5 ms (including network time), then on average 2,000 × 0.005 = 10 connections are in use. A pool of 20 to 30 gives headroom for bursts and variance. A pool of 200 adds nothing: the extra connections sit idle, or, worse, under a burst they all become active at once and the database's work per query rises.

The upper bound comes from the database's capacity. The HikariCP guide's starting formula for a single database is connections = (core_count × 2) + effective_spindle_count, where the spindle term accounts for I/O waits on spinning disks (for SSD-backed or fully cached data it is near zero). The reasoning: with no I/O waits, a core can only run one query at a time, so connections beyond the core count just time-slice; I/O waits let a few more connections keep the CPUs busy. For a 16-core database that suggests roughly 32 active connections in total, which is far fewer than most teams configure. Their benchmark chart of PostgreSQL throughput flattens around 50 connections.

Two consequences follow. The limit is total active connections across all application instances, so pool size per instance must be divided accordingly: 10 instances × 20 connections = 200, already several times too many for a 16-core database. And the cost of holding a connection grows with everything done while holding it, so the most effective way to need fewer connections is to hold each for less time: shorter transactions, no external calls inside them, fewer round trips per transaction.

3. Poolers: PgBouncer and its modes

Application-side pools work per process. With many processes (a Python service running 200 worker processes, serverless functions that each open their own connection), the total still explodes. An external pooler sits between applications and the database and multiplexes: thousands of client connections to the pooler, a few dozen server connections from the pooler to PostgreSQL. PgBouncer is the standard choice; cloud providers offer managed equivalents. Its default_pool_size is 20 server connections per user and database pair, and its pool_mode decides when a server connection returns to the pool:

  • Session (the default): a client keeps its server connection until it disconnects. Safe for all features, but provides little multiplexing; it mostly saves connection setup time.
  • Transaction: a client gets a server connection only for the duration of each transaction. Between transactions, the same server connection may serve other clients. This is the mode that makes thousands of clients share a few dozen connections.
  • Statement: a server connection is returned after every statement, so multi-statement transactions are not allowed. Rarely used.

Transaction mode has one important consequence: session state does not survive between transactions, because the next transaction may run on a different server connection. Anything that lives in the session breaks: a plain SET search_path or SET timezone (use SET LOCAL inside the transaction, or set defaults on the role), temporary tables, session-level advisory locks (use transaction-level ones), LISTEN/NOTIFY, and cursors held across transactions. Named prepared statements were historically a problem too; PgBouncer 1.21 added tracking of protocol-level prepared statements in transaction mode, enabled with max_prepared_statements. Knowing this list prevents a class of bugs that appear only after a pooler is introduced.

4. Transactions in request code

Each request should treat a transaction as a short, precise unit: begin, do the reads and writes that must be atomic, commit. The rules that keep systems healthy are simple to state and easy to violate through frameworks:

Never hold a transaction across external work. An HTTP call to a payment provider, a message-queue publish, a file upload or an LLM request can take seconds. During that time the transaction holds its row locks (blocking other writers, db9), its snapshot (blocking vacuum, db10), and its connection (unavailable to the pool). Structure the code as: short transaction to read and perhaps reserve; commit; external call; short transaction to record the result. To make the second transaction safe against concurrent changes, use an optimistic version check or a status transition (UPDATE … WHERE status = 'pending').

Know where your framework starts transactions. Some frameworks wrap each request in a transaction automatically (Django's ATOMIC_REQUESTS, many Spring @Transactional configurations); then an external call anywhere in the request is inside it. Others use autocommit until told otherwise. Read the configuration and make transaction boundaries explicit in important paths.

Set timeouts on the database side. statement_timeout caps any single statement; idle_in_transaction_session_timeout terminates sessions that opened a transaction and stopped sending commands; lock_timeout caps waits for locks. Set them per role, so application roles get tight limits and migration or analytics roles get looser ones. Without them, one bug can hold locks and snapshots indefinitely.

5. How ORMs turn code into SQL

An ORM maps classes to tables and objects to rows. session.get(Post, 42) becomes SELECT … FROM post WHERE id = 42; changing post.title and committing becomes an UPDATE; post.author is a relationship mapped through the author_id foreign key. Two ORM mechanisms matter most for performance. The unit of work tracks changes to loaded objects and writes them together at flush or commit, which is convenient but means writes happen later than the line of code that caused them. And relationship loading decides when related objects are fetched, which is where N+1 comes from.

By default, most ORMs use lazy loading for relationships: post.author issues SELECT … FROM author WHERE id = ? the first time it is accessed. In isolation that is reasonable. In a loop over 100 posts, it is 100 extra queries. The alternatives are eager loading strategies, named differently in each ORM but the same two ideas:

StrategySQL shapeSQLAlchemyDjangoRails
Joinone query, LEFT JOIN related tablejoinedloadselect_relatedeager_load
Batched second queryparent query, then WHERE id IN (…)selectinloadprefetch_relatedpreload

Use the join for to-one relationships (each post has one author), where it adds columns but not rows. Use the batched IN query for to-many relationships (each post has many comments), where a join would repeat each post's columns once per comment and multiply rows (the db3 fan-out), and where a LIMIT on posts would cut off comments.

6. Counting an N+1, worked

The lab renders a page of 100 posts with their author names three ways, on a table of a million posts and 10,000 authors. The lazy version runs one query for the posts and then one per post for its author: 101 queries. The batched version runs the posts query and one SELECT … WHERE id IN (…) with the distinct author ids: 2 queries. The join version runs 1 query.

Because SQLite runs inside the Python process, all three are fast in the lab (about 0.5, 0.3 and 0.1 ms), which is exactly why N+1 hides in development with a local database. Add a realistic network round trip of 0.5 ms per query, as the lab does arithmetically, and the picture changes: about 51 ms for the lazy version, 1.3 ms for the batched version, 0.6 ms for the join. The query work is identical; the difference is 99 round trips. With a database in another availability zone (1-2 ms round trips) the lazy page takes 100-200 ms. And the count scales with the data: a page that lists 500 items with two lazy relationships each makes 1,001 queries.

N+1 has variants that are harder to spot: a template that touches order.customer.address.city fires three lazy loads per row; a serializer that includes a nested relationship; a loop that calls a helper which queries one row at a time; a GraphQL resolver per field. The defence is measurement. Count queries per request in tests and fail when a budget is exceeded, which is what GitLab's query count limit does with a default of 100 per controller, endpoint or worker; Django's assertNumQueries, Rails' Bullet gem and Python's nplusone library automate it. In production, pg_stat_statements shows a query shape such as SELECT … FROM author WHERE id = $1 with a call count far higher than the request rate, which is the signature of N+1.

7. OFFSET pagination and its costs

The simplest way to page through a sorted list is ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 100 OFFSET 900000 for page 9,001. With an index on (created_at, id), the database walks the index in order, but it must still step over the first 900,000 entries and discard them before returning the next 100: OFFSET is not a jump, it is a count. The lab measures it on a million posts: about 25 ms for that page, against about 0.1 ms for the first page, and the cost grows linearly with depth. Without a usable index it is worse: the database sorts the whole table (or keeps a top-N heap of 900,100 rows) for every page request.

OFFSET also gives wrong results when data changes between requests. A user reads page 1 (rows 1-100); a new row is inserted at the top; they request page 2 with OFFSET 100 and see row 100 again, now shifted to position 101. Deletes cause the opposite: a row is skipped. For feeds that update constantly, users see duplicates and gaps.

8. Keyset pagination

Keyset pagination (also called seek pagination) remembers where the previous page ended instead of how many rows to skip. The sort order must be total, meaning no two rows can tie, which is guaranteed by appending a unique column (usually the primary key) to the sort: ORDER BY created_at, id. The first page is an ordinary LIMIT 100. Each following page uses the last row's sort key values:

SELECT id, title FROM post
WHERE (created_at, id) > ($last_created_at, $last_id)
ORDER BY created_at, id
LIMIT 100;

The row-value comparison (a, b) > (x, y) means "a > x, or a = x and b > y", which is exactly "after the last row in sort order", and an index on (created_at, id) serves it as one descent to the starting point followed by reading 100 entries. The lab's keyset query returns the same 100 rows as OFFSET 900000 (the script asserts it) in about 0.1 ms, the same as the first page. Every page costs the same at any depth, and inserts or deletes elsewhere do not shift pages, because each page is anchored to a key, not a position. For descending feeds, flip the comparison and the sort: WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC.

Two practical notes. Some databases do not optimise row-value comparisons well (older MySQL versions in particular); the equivalent expanded form, WHERE created_at > $1 OR (created_at = $1 AND id > $2), works everywhere but may need care to use the index. And APIs should not expose raw keys: encode the last key as an opaque cursor string (often base64 of a small JSON object, sometimes signed), returned with each page and passed back for the next, which also lets the server change the sort key later. Keyset pagination gives up jumping to page 37 directly and exact total page counts; most feeds and APIs need only next and previous, and totals can be estimates.

9. Bulk writes and round trips

The N+1 lesson applies to writes too. Inserting 10,000 rows with 10,000 separate INSERT statements in autocommit mode costs 10,000 round trips and 10,000 commits, each a WAL flush (db8). The same rows in one transaction cost one commit; as one multi-row INSERT … VALUES (…), (…), … per few hundred rows, a few dozen round trips; via PostgreSQL's COPY (or the driver's bulk API), a single streaming operation that is typically an order of magnitude faster still. ORMs have bulk APIs (bulk_create, insert_many, SQLAlchemy's executemany "insertmanyvalues" mode) that bypass per-object overhead. For updates, a single UPDATE … FROM (VALUES …) or an update joined to a temporary table replaces thousands of per-row statements. Background jobs that backfill or migrate data should always batch, typically 1,000 to 10,000 rows per transaction, small enough to keep locks and transactions short and large enough to amortise round trips (db14).

10. Parameters, prepared statements and injection

Every query that includes a value from outside should send that value as a bound parameter, not by string concatenation: cursor.execute("SELECT … WHERE email = %s", (email,)), never f"… WHERE email = '{email}'". Concatenation lets input such as ' OR '1'='1 become part of the SQL, which is SQL injection, still one of the most exploited vulnerability classes (swe13). Parameters are sent separately from the SQL text, so they can never change its structure. ORMs parameterise automatically; raw SQL helpers inside ORMs (text(), raw()) need explicit parameters. Identifiers (table or column names chosen at run time) cannot be parameters and must be validated against an allow-list.

Bound parameters also enable prepared statements: the server parses and plans a statement once and executes it many times with different values, saving planning time for frequent queries. The trade-offs are the generic-plan issue for skewed data (db7) and the session-state issue with transaction-mode poolers (section 3). For LLM features that generate SQL (text-to-SQL), the same principles apply with more force: run generated queries through a read-only role with tight timeouts, never interpolate user or model text into SQL outside parameters, and validate the statement shape before execution.

11. Reading less: projections, streaming and caching

Round trips are one cost; the volume of each response is another. ORMs load whole objects by default, every column of every row, including large text and JSON columns that the page never shows. Selecting only the needed columns (SQLAlchemy's load_only, Django's only or values, Rails' select or pluck) shrinks network transfer and, more importantly, the CPU and memory spent building objects, which for large result sets often exceeds the query time itself. When a job must process millions of rows, fetch them with a server-side cursor or in keyset-ordered batches rather than loading the whole result into memory, so memory stays flat and the first rows are processed while later ones are still being read.

Caching removes queries entirely, at the price of staleness. Read-mostly reference data (plans, model price lists, feature flags) can be cached in process for seconds to minutes; per-user or per-tenant data can be cached in Redis with explicit invalidation on write. The common bug is caching inside a transaction-sensitive path, for example reading a cached balance and then writing a new one, which reintroduces the lost update that row locks were preventing (db9). Cache values you only display; read authoritative values inside the transaction that changes them.

12. Retries and idempotency

Database calls fail transiently: connections drop during failovers, serialization failures and deadlocks abort transactions (db9), statements time out. Retrying is correct only when the operation is safe to repeat. Reads are. A whole transaction aborted by a serialization failure or deadlock is (it did nothing), so the retry must re-run the entire transaction, including its reads. The dangerous case is an ambiguous failure: the connection dropped after the client sent COMMIT but before the response arrived. The transaction may or may not have committed, and blindly retrying an insert can create a duplicate order or a second charge.

The standard fix is an idempotency key: the client generates a unique key per logical operation, the server stores it under a unique constraint in the same transaction as the operation's effects, along with the result, and a retry with the same key finds the stored result and returns it instead of acting again. Natural unique constraints achieve the same where they exist (one payment per invoice id). Combine with retry policies that retry only known-transient errors (connection errors, SQLSTATE 40001 and 40P01), use exponential backoff with jitter, and cap attempts. For LLM agents, whose steps are often retried by an orchestrator, an idempotency key per tool call is what prevents a retried step from writing the same result twice.
deep:
Why too many connections hurt PostgreSQL specifically

Beyond generic CPU time-slicing, PostgreSQL has structural reasons to dislike many active connections. Computing a snapshot (db9) historically required scanning an array with an entry for every backend, so snapshot cost grew with connection count; PostgreSQL 14 substantially improved this, making many idle connections much cheaper, but active ones still contend. Every backend that touches shared buffers, the lock manager, the WAL insertion locks or the proc array takes lightweight locks (LWLocks) on shared structures, and with hundreds of active backends those locks become hot. Each backend also keeps private caches of catalog data and plans, so memory grows with connections times schema size; databases with thousands of tables (common in multi-tenant schema-per-tenant designs) can spend gigabytes on per-backend caches. The pooling answer is not just about connection setup cost; it is about keeping the number of simultaneously active backends near the hardware's real parallelism.

Queueing theory behind pool sizing

Little's law gives the average, but latency depends on variance. As utilisation of a server approaches 100%, queueing delay grows sharply (for a simple single-server queue, waiting time is proportional to ρ / (1 − ρ), where ρ is utilisation), so a database running at 95% has far longer queues than one at 70%. Pool limits decide where that queue forms. With a small pool, excess requests queue in the application, where the wait is cheap (an idle coroutine or thread), visible in pool metrics, and bounded by a timeout that can shed load gracefully. With a huge pool, the queue forms inside the database as runnable backends and lock waiters, where waiting is expensive and slows everyone. This is the same insight as the HikariCP and Oracle demonstrations, stated generally: put the queue in front of the bottleneck, not inside it. It also suggests what to monitor: pool wait time and pool timeouts are the leading indicators that the database, not the application, needs more capacity or less work.

The ORM impedance mismatch

Object graphs and relational tables represent data differently, and every ORM pays for bridging them. Objects navigate by reference (order.customer.address); tables relate by keys and are queried in sets. Objects have identity (the same customer object should appear once in memory however many orders reference it), which ORMs maintain with an identity map per session; tables have only key values. Objects have inheritance; tables need one of the subtype mappings from db1. Lazy loading is the ORM's way of making references navigable without loading the whole database, and N+1 is its natural failure mode. The practical stance most experienced teams adopt is to use the ORM for writes and simple reads (where identity maps, unit of work and validation help), configure eager loading deliberately per use case, and write SQL (or the ORM's query builder at the SQL level) for reporting, bulk operations and anything performance-critical. Treat the generated SQL as an output to review, not an implementation detail.

Pagination beyond the basics

Several refinements of keyset pagination come up in practice. Sorting by a non-unique column (price, score) always needs the unique tie-breaker, and the index must include it in the same order. Sorting by a computed or mutable value (relevance, a like count that changes) means the key of the last seen row may have changed by the next request; feeds either snapshot the ranking (store ranked ids for the session) or accept small inconsistencies. Backward pagination reverses comparison and order, then reverses the result in the application. Totals: exact COUNT(*) over large filtered sets is expensive in MVCC databases (no cached count; db9), so many products show estimates from planner statistics (EXPLAIN's row estimate or pg_class.reltuples) or "more than 10,000". For search results ranked by a relevance score in a search engine, deep pagination is usually capped altogether, because computing the 10,000th result exactly requires scoring and sorting everything before it.

Serverless and connection management

Serverless functions and autoscaling containers make connection management harder: each instance opens its own pool, instances appear and disappear by the hundred, and a traffic spike can create thousands of connections in seconds. The patterns that cope are an external pooler or managed proxy (such as PgBouncer or a cloud provider's database proxy) that absorbs client connections, very small per-instance pools (often 1-2), aggressive idle timeouts so dying instances release connections, and HTTP-based database APIs for some serverless databases that avoid persistent connections entirely. The capacity rule does not change: total active connections must stay near what the database can run in parallel.
prod:
The pool-sizing incident pattern

A recognisable incident: traffic grows, latency rises, someone raises the application's pool size from 20 to 100 per instance "to handle more load", and latency gets worse, sometimes catastrophically, because the database is now running several times more active queries than it has cores, contending on locks and memory. The Oracle demonstration cited by HikariCP is the canonical illustration: shrinking the pool from 2,048 to 96 connections improved response times about fiftyfold. The diagnostic signals are many active backends in pg_stat_activity with wait events on LWLocks or locks, database CPU not saturated by useful work, rising context switches, and application pool metrics showing connections busy but slow. The fix is the reverse of the instinct: reduce total connections to a small multiple of cores, add a pooler in transaction mode if there are many application processes, and let excess requests wait in the application, where they can be shed with timeouts.

Connection storms and exhaustion

The opposite failure is running out. PostgreSQL's max_connections (100 by default) is a hard limit, with a few slots reserved for superusers; when it is reached, new connections fail with "too many clients". Common triggers are a deploy that briefly doubles instances (old and new both running), a retry loop that opens new connections on every failure, connection leaks (code paths that borrow and never return, especially on exceptions), and idle-in-transaction sessions that hold connections indefinitely. Defences: a pooler in front, pool limits sized for deployments, leak detection in the pool library (HikariCP's leak detection threshold, SQLAlchemy's pool logging), always returning connections in finally or context managers, and alerts on connection counts by state and by application name (set application_name per service so pg_stat_activity shows who owns what).

Query budgets and visibility

GitLab's query count limit is an example of a cheap, effective guardrail: tests fail when an endpoint exceeds 100 queries, and exceptions require choosing an explicit higher threshold, so N+1 regressions are caught in code review rather than in production. Complementary production tooling: application performance monitoring that shows queries per request and the call sites that issued them; pg_stat_statements to find query shapes with call counts out of proportion to traffic; and slow-query logging with auto_explain for the long tail. A useful dashboard metric is "queries per request" per endpoint over time; a step change after a deploy is almost always a new lazy load.

Pagination in public APIs

Public APIs that started with page numbers often migrate to cursors when datasets grow: deep OFFSET pages become slow enough to time out, and integrators syncing data with page numbers miss or duplicate records as data changes during the sync. The migration path is to add cursor-based pagination alongside page numbers, cap the maximum OFFSET (for example, refuse pages beyond 100), and document that cursors are opaque. For data export use cases, offer a dedicated bulk export (a file or a change feed) rather than encouraging clients to page through millions of records.

Patterns for LLM-backed services

LLM features stress every topic in this lesson. Request durations are long (seconds of generation), so any transaction or connection held across a model call multiplies connection needs by orders of magnitude: a service doing 50 requests per second with a 4-second model call inside a transaction needs about 200 connections by Little's law; with the model call outside, perhaps 2. Agent loops issue many small database operations per step, which are prone to N+1 patterns over tool results. Streaming responses tempt per-token writes; batch them. Retries are common (rate limits, timeouts), so idempotency keys per request and per tool call are essential. And conversation history reads are a natural keyset pagination: load the last 50 messages by (conversation_id, seq) descending, then older ones on demand, never by OFFSET.
myths: A bigger connection pool means more throughput.

The database can only run as many queries at once as it has cores and I/O capacity; beyond that, extra connections add context switching, lock contention and memory. The HikariCP pool-sizing guide recounts an Oracle demonstration where cutting the pool from 2,048 connections to 96 cut response times from about 100 ms to about 2 ms. Size pools from the database's capacity, not from the number of application threads.
ORMs generate inefficient SQL, so serious teams avoid them.

ORMs generate perfectly good SQL for most queries; the problems come from loading patterns (lazy loading in loops), fetching whole objects when a few columns are needed, and hiding where transactions start and end. Teams that use ORMs well read the generated SQL for important paths, configure eager loading, and drop to hand-written SQL where it matters.
N+1 queries only matter at large scale.

The cost is round trips: 101 queries at half a millisecond of network latency each is 50 ms before any query does real work, on a page that could have taken 1 ms. It matters on day one, and it grows silently as lists get longer, because the number of queries grows with the data, not the code.
OFFSET pagination is fine because the database uses an index.

OFFSET 900000 still has to walk past 900,000 entries before returning the next 100, so deep pages get linearly slower; the lab measured about 25 ms versus about 0.1 ms for the keyset equivalent. OFFSET pages also skip or repeat rows when data is inserted or deleted between page requests.
Wrapping each request in one big transaction is the safe default.

A transaction held across slow work (external API calls, LLM requests, user think time) holds locks and an old snapshot, blocking writers and vacuum. Transactions should cover exactly the database work that must be atomic and nothing else; many requests need several small transactions, not one large one.
Retries make database writes reliable.

Retries make transient failures survivable only if the retried operation is safe to repeat. Retrying a non-idempotent insert after a timeout can create duplicates, because the first attempt may have committed. Use idempotency keys or unique constraints so a retry is detected, and retry only on errors known to be retryable.
lab:
Goal: count the queries and time of N+1 versus batched versus joined loading, and compare OFFSET with keyset pagination on a deep page, using a million-row SQLite table. Python 3.12 standard library. Save as db13.py; building the table takes a few seconds.

import random, sqlite3, time

random.seed(13)
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE author (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE post (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, author_id INT, created_at INT, title TEXT);
CREATE INDEX post_created ON post (created_at, id);
""")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO author VALUES (?, ?)", [(a, f"author{a}") for a in range(10_000)])
db.executemany("INSERT INTO post VALUES (?,?,?,?)",
               [(p, random.randrange(10_000), p, f"post {p}") for p in range(1_000_000)])

queries = 0
def q(sql, args=()):
    global queries
    queries += 1
    return db.execute(sql, args).fetchall()

def timed(label, fn):
    global queries
    queries = 0
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); fn(); ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000
    rtt = 0.5                                          # ms per round trip to a networked DB
    print(f"{label:<34} {queries:>4} queries  {ms:7.2f} ms in-process"
          f"  ~{ms + queries * rtt:6.1f} ms over a 0.5 ms network")

# Part 1: render a page of 100 posts with their author names
def n_plus_one():
    posts = q("SELECT id, author_id, title FROM post ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 100")
    for _, author_id, _ in posts:                      # one query per post: the N
        q("SELECT name FROM author WHERE id = ?", (author_id,))
def batched():
    posts = q("SELECT id, author_id, title FROM post ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 100")
    ids = sorted({a for _, a, _ in posts})
    q(f"SELECT id, name FROM author WHERE id IN ({','.join('?' * len(ids))})", ids)
def joined():
    q("""SELECT p.id, a.name, p.title FROM post p JOIN author a ON a.id = p.author_id
         ORDER BY p.created_at DESC LIMIT 100""")
timed("N+1 (lazy loading)", n_plus_one)
timed("batched IN (selectin loading)", batched)
timed("single JOIN (joined loading)", joined)

# Part 2: page 9,000 of 100 rows: OFFSET versus keyset
def offset_page():
    q("SELECT id, title FROM post ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 100 OFFSET 900000")
last = db.execute("SELECT created_at, id FROM post ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 1 OFFSET 899999").fetchone()
def keyset_page():
    q("""SELECT id, title FROM post WHERE (created_at, id) > (?, ?)
         ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 100""", last)
timed("OFFSET 900000 LIMIT 100", offset_page)
timed("keyset WHERE (ts, id) > last", keyset_page)
assert db.execute("SELECT id FROM post ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 100 OFFSET 900000").fetchall() == \
       db.execute("SELECT id FROM post WHERE (created_at, id) > (?, ?) ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 100", last).fetchall()
print("same 100 rows either way")

What to look for.

  1. The lazy version issues 101 queries, the batched version 2, the join 1. In-process timings are all under a millisecond, which is why N+1 hides on a laptop; the estimate with a 0.5 ms network round trip shows about 51 ms versus about 1.3 ms and 0.6 ms.
  2. OFFSET 900000 takes about 25 ms; the keyset query takes about 0.1 ms and returns the same 100 rows (the script asserts this). Rerun with OFFSET 100000 and 500000 to see the linear growth; the keyset time does not change.

Try next. Change the 0.5 ms round trip to 2 ms (a cross-zone database) and recompute the N+1 total. Add a second lazy relationship (for example a category per post) and count queries again: 201. Then insert a new post with a timestamp before the last key between fetching two OFFSET pages and between two keyset pages, and observe that OFFSET repeats a row while keyset does not.
recap: A database connection is an expensive server-side resource (a whole process in PostgreSQL), so applications reuse a small number of them through a connection pool.
Little's law sizes pools: connections busy at once equal throughput times time spent per transaction, so 2,000 transactions per second at 5 ms each keeps about 10 connections busy.
Throughput peaks at a pool size near a small multiple of the database's cores; larger pools increase latency without adding throughput.
PgBouncer multiplexes many client connections onto few server connections; transaction pooling gives the best reuse but breaks session state such as SET, temporary tables and session advisory locks.
An N+1 query pattern runs one query for a list and then one more per item, usually from ORM lazy loading in a loop; fix it with a join or a batched IN query, and enforce query-count budgets in tests.

OFFSET pagination reads and discards all skipped rows and is unstable under concurrent writes; keyset pagination continues from the last seen sort key with an indexed WHERE condition and costs the same at any depth.
Keep transactions short, never span network calls or model calls, set statement and idle-in-transaction timeouts, and make writes idempotent so retries are safe.
Use bound parameters (prepared statements) for every query, both for safety against SQL injection and for plan reuse.
Batch writes (multi-row INSERT, COPY, executemany in one transaction) to turn thousands of round trips and commits into a few.
glossary: A set of open database connections kept by the application (or a proxy) and lent to requests, avoiding the cost of opening a connection per request.
An opaque token returned to API clients that encodes the last seen sort key, used to fetch the next page.
Loading related objects together with the main query, by a join or a batched second query, instead of on first access.
A client-supplied unique key for an operation, stored with its result so a retried request returns the original result instead of repeating the action.
Fetching the next page with WHERE sort_key > last_seen_key ORDER BY sort_key LIMIT n, served by an index; also called seek pagination.
An ORM behaviour where related objects are fetched only when first accessed, issuing a query at that moment.
In a stable system, the average number of items in it equals arrival rate times average time each spends in it.
One query to fetch N items followed by one query per item to fetch related data, N+1 round trips in total.
Fetching page k with LIMIT n OFFSET k×n, which makes the database skip k×n rows each time.
Object-relational mapper: a library mapping table rows to program objects and generating SQL from code (SQLAlchemy, Django ORM, Hibernate, ActiveRecord, Prisma).
A lightweight PostgreSQL connection pooler that runs as a proxy and multiplexes client connections onto a few server connections.
PgBouncer's rule for when a server connection returns to the pool: after the session, the transaction, or each statement.
A SQL statement sent once with placeholders and executed many times with bound parameter values.
One request from the application to the database and the response back; its network latency is paid per query.
A database cursor that streams a large result to the client in chunks instead of sending it all at once.
Settings and objects tied to one database connection, such as SET parameters, temporary tables, prepared statements and session advisory locks.
An attack where user input is interpreted as SQL because it was concatenated into a query string instead of bound as a parameter.
A limit on how long one statement may run before the database cancels it.
Transport Layer Security: the encryption and authentication layer used for database connections over the network.
An ORM pattern that tracks changes to loaded objects and writes them in one flush, usually inside one transaction.
drill:
Diagnose: the dashboard endpoint that melts the database at 9 a.m.

A Python service (40 instances, each with SQLAlchemy pool_size=20, max_overflow=30) serves an admin dashboard. Every morning at 9:00 latency goes from 150 ms to 8 s and the database (16 cores) shows 600-900 active connections. The endpoint loads the user's 50 projects, and for each project displays its owner's name, its last 5 runs, and the run's model name. Projects list pages use OFFSET. Explain what is happening and fix it at the pool, query and pagination levels.

Answer

Pool. 40 instances × (20 + 30 overflow) allows up to 2,000 connections; at the 9:00 spike, hundreds become active on a 16-core database, and latency explodes from contention, not from real work. Size from capacity: target roughly 32-48 active connections in total; with 40 instances that is about 1 per instance, so put PgBouncer in transaction mode in front, set each instance's pool to about 5 with no overflow, and let requests queue with a pool timeout. Check for transactions held across slow work (any external calls in the request).

Queries. The page is a nested N+1: 1 query for projects, 50 for owners, 50 for runs, and up to 250 for run models: about 351 queries per page view, 175 ms of round trips at 0.5 ms each before any work, and hundreds of connection borrow-and-return cycles. Rewrite: projects with owners in one join (joinedload); the last 5 runs per project in one query using a window function or LATERAL (db4): SELECT … FROM project p CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT … FROM run r WHERE r.project_id = p.id ORDER BY r.created_at DESC LIMIT 5) r WHERE p.owner_id = $1, with an index on run(project_id, created_at DESC); models via a join or a cached lookup table. Total: 2-3 queries. Add a query-count assertion to the endpoint's test (budget of, say, 10).

Pagination. Replace OFFSET with keyset on (updated_at, id) and an opaque cursor; deep pages become as cheap as the first, and pages stay stable as projects update.

Verify. After the change, active connections should stay near the pool cap, p99 latency should drop below the original 150 ms, and pg_stat_statements call counts for the owner and model lookups should fall by roughly fiftyfold.
qa: E
Why do applications use connection pools?

Opening a database connection costs a TCP and TLS handshake, authentication and, in PostgreSQL, forking a server process with its own memory, often several milliseconds. A pool keeps a few connections open and lends them to requests, so each request pays only the cost of borrowing one. It also caps how many connections the application can open, protecting the database.
E
What is the N+1 query problem?

Code fetches a list of N items with one query, then, in a loop, triggers one more query per item to load related data (each post's author, each order's customer), N+1 queries in all. It usually comes from ORM lazy loading. Each query costs a network round trip, so 100 items mean 101 round trips instead of one or two.
E
What is wrong with OFFSET pagination for deep pages?

To return rows 900,001-900,100, the database must find and discard the first 900,000 rows in sort order, so page cost grows linearly with depth. And if rows are inserted or deleted between requests, OFFSET pages shift, so users see duplicates or miss rows.
M
How would you size a connection pool for a service doing 3,000 transactions per second, each holding a connection for about 4 ms, on a 16-core database?

Little's law: connections in use = 3,000 per second × 0.004 s = 12 on average. Add headroom for bursts and variance, perhaps 20-30 in total across all instances, and check that this is within a small multiple of the database's 16 cores. With 10 application instances that is 2-3 connections each, which surprises people who default to 20 per instance (200 total).

Follow-up: What if the pool is exhausted? — Requests wait for a connection up to a timeout; that wait is queueing you can see in pool metrics, and it is better than 200 connections all contending inside the database.
M
Fix this N+1 in an ORM: for post in Post.query.limit(100): print(post.author.name).

Eager-load the relationship: a join (SQLAlchemy joinedload, Django select_related, Rails eager_load) returns posts with their authors in one query; or a batched second query (SQLAlchemy selectinload, Django prefetch_related, Rails preload) loads all needed authors with one WHERE id IN (...). Use the join for to-one relationships and small results, the IN batch for to-many relationships, where a join would repeat parent rows.
M
Write keyset pagination for a feed ordered by created_at descending.

First page: SELECT … FROM post ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20. Next page, given the last row's (created_at, id): SELECT … WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20, with an index on (created_at, id). The id tie-breaker makes the order total, so rows with equal timestamps are neither skipped nor repeated; the API returns the last key as an opaque cursor.

Follow-up: What do you lose versus OFFSET? — Jumping to an arbitrary page number and showing 'page 37 of 912'; for most feeds and APIs, next and previous are all users need, and the total count is often an estimate anyway.
M
What are PgBouncer's pool modes and what breaks in transaction mode?

Session mode gives a client a server connection for its whole session (safe, little multiplexing); transaction mode lends one only for each transaction (high multiplexing); statement mode for each statement (no multi-statement transactions). In transaction mode, anything tied to the session breaks across transactions: SET without LOCAL, temporary tables, session advisory locks, LISTEN, and historically named prepared statements, which PgBouncer 1.21+ can track with max_prepared_statements.
M
Why should a request never hold a transaction open while calling an external API or an LLM?

The transaction keeps its row locks and its snapshot for the whole call, which can take seconds: other writers to those rows wait, deadlock chances rise, vacuum cannot clean anything newer than the snapshot, and the connection is unavailable to the pool. Read what you need, commit, make the call, then write the result in a new short transaction guarded by a version check or idempotency key.
M
How do you make a 'create payment' endpoint safe to retry?

Require an idempotency key from the client. In one transaction, insert the key into an idempotency table with a unique constraint and the request hash, perform the write, and store the response. A retry with the same key hits the unique constraint, and the handler returns the stored response instead of charging again. Retry only on transient errors (connection loss, serialization failure, deadlock), with backoff.
H
A service's p99 latency jumps under load while database CPU is only 40%. The pool has 100 connections per instance across 30 instances. What is happening?

Up to 3,000 connections can be active; PostgreSQL handles each as a process, and with that many active backends, contention on locks and shared structures, context switching and memory pressure dominate, so queries slow down although no single resource is saturated by real work. Reduce pool sizes so total active connections are a few times the core count, put PgBouncer in transaction mode in front, and let requests queue in the application pool, where the wait is visible and cheap.

Follow-up: How do you show the pool is the problem? — Compare pg_stat_activity (many active backends with lock or LWLock waits) with application metrics of pool wait time; after shrinking pools, throughput should hold and p99 fall.
H
Your ORM loads 5,000 order objects to compute a total, and the endpoint takes two seconds. Fix it at three levels.

Query level: compute the aggregate in SQL, SELECT SUM(total) FROM orders WHERE …, returning one row instead of 5,000 objects. ORM level: when objects are needed, select only required columns (load_only, values(), pluck) and stream with server-side cursors instead of materialising everything.
